entries.title: Texas District Attorney Launches Investigation Into Potentially Fraudulent Mailers
entries.summary: The pamphlets, which guide children seeking gender-affirming care, were reportedly sent by a company in Wyoming — not by the trans rights organization listed on the mailers.
entries.content:
A Republican district attorney in West Texas has opened a forgery investigation into pamphlets mailed to voters this month containing information for transgender students, claiming to be sent by a trans rights organization.

The pamphlets in question detail information about what children can do to receive gender-affirming care and legal emancipation, as well as steps a student can take if their parents don’t support having a trans child.

The pamphlets state they were sent out by Transgender Education Network of Texas but the organization denied it had distributed the mailers. The Texas Tribune reported this week that the pamphlets were sent out by a limited liability company in Wyoming, and that the transgender rights group had received backlash and violent threats.

Sarah Stogner, the district attorney for several West Texas counties, confirmed to The Washington Sun she was launching a probe.

“It’s worth investigating and mailers were sent in my district so I have jurisdiction to investigate potential forgery,” Stogner told The Sun in an email. “I don’t want to speculate on any other conclusions at this time.”

The investigation comes after Republican state Rep. Jeff Leach sent two letters calling for state Attorney General Ken Paxton to investigate the origin of the mailers.

The Tribune first reported about the investigation. Stogner told the news outlet that she felt the mailers were an obvious bid to agitate voters ahead of the midterms, though their origin is currently unknown.

entries.title: Ilhan Omar’s Campaign Raised $1.9 Million in the First Two Weeks of October
entries.summary: The Minnesota Democrat pulled in more than $172,000 alone on the day federal agents raided her D.C. home.
entries.content:
Rep. Ilhan Omar raised nearly $1.9 million for her reelection campaign in the first two weeks of October, a haul that coincided with a federal raid on her Washington, D.C., home and her efforts to capitalize on what she called an “authoritarian attack.”

More than 1,300 itemized donations totaling more than $172,000 poured in Oct. 12, a Federal Election Commission filing shows, the day the Minnesota Democrat was awakened by federal agents serving a search warrant for what the Justice Department called an “ongoing federal criminal investigation.” That’s nearly 100 times the amount she raised a week before.

Omar’s campaign had brought in about $520,000 in contributions in the two months prior.

Omar’s campaign had fundraised off the raid, asking supporters for donations the night of Oct. 12 by saying the DOJ action was “a dangerous and authoritarian attack on a political opponent.”

“We have an obligation to fight back against this ludicrous, partisan investigation, and show that we will not let Trump’s abuse of power go unchecked,” the email said.

Since federal agents entered her home, Omar’s campaign has sent supporters 11 emails referencing the raid, according to PoliticalEmails.org.

Omar noted the wave of support on TikTok earlier this week, saying the donations would go “a long way as we fight Trump and his administration for trying to intimidate me and so many people right before the midterm elections.”

Following the raid, President Donald Trump said while he was not involved in the case against Omar she was a “terrible person.”

Trump posted to Truth Social on Thursday night to demand Omar’s resignation for using a “fake name” while being sworn in, a reference to a court filing by the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, Jeanine Pirro. The president said Omar “will not be legally allowed to be a Member … from this point forth,” though he has no power to remove her from Congress.

entries.title: Trump’s Battle With the Media Ramps Up
entries.summary: This week brought a retraction demand to Politico, a reporter blocked from Air Force One, an FCC warning to broadcasters and a reported plan to evict the press corps from the White House.
entries.content:
As President Donald Trump barnstorms the country ahead of the midterms, on top of his usual White House events this week, he’s had some pointed exchanges with journalists in his path. He called one reporter a “dummy,” another “a stupid person” and a third “a sick person.”

The angry name-calling comes as tensions between the White House and the media have ratcheted up.

The White House this week demanded a retraction from Politico under threat of reviewing the publication’s access, blocked a reporter with The Independent from joining the president’s travel pool after a heated exchange in the Oval Office and declined to rule out evicting the press corps from the building altogether. The FCC’s chair warned broadcasters that airing “Fake Polls” could put them crosswise with their licensing obligations.

White House counsel Will Scharf sent a letter to Politico’s global editor-in-chief, Jonathan Greenberger, on Monday demanding the retraction and removal of three articles about chief of staff Susie Wiles within 48 hours and warning of a potential review of Politico's White House access. It coincided with ongoing litigation between the news organization and the White House. Politico, CNN and MS NOW had their hard passes revoked in September, which were reinstated via an Oct. 13 injunction that’s under appeal. (The Washington Sun has signed onto an amicus brief filed in this case in support of the news outlets.)

As Axios first reported, Scharf accused the outlet of publishing “demonstrably false and defamatory articles in an apparent effort to manufacture a narrative of dysfunction and infighting.” The targeted pieces included two Playbook items concerning potential calls to replace Wiles and a subsequent White House reaction, alongside an Oct. 16 article about Wiles' role in arranging former press secretary Katie Zacharia's Fox News interview with Sean Hannity.

Politico published a new version of the Wiles–Zacharia story on Wednesday evening. The correction at the top of the article said the previous version, including its headline, “mischaracterized the role” Wiles played and Politico’s “follow-up reporting indicates she did not play a direct role in setting up the interview.” The outlet appended the same language to Thursday’s Playbook and to a post on X replacing an earlier one.

It left the other two items alone. In a letter to Scharf dated Tuesday and reviewed by The Washington Sun, attorney Theodore J. Boutrous Jr. wrote that Politico “categorically rejects the false accusations” and had reexamined all three articles before concluding one warranted correction. The timing and substance of the demand, Boutrous wrote, “further confirms the unlawful retaliatory and viewpoint discriminatory motives” behind the September ban.

The White House was unmoved. “Politico should apologize to its dwindling readership for knowingly publishing lies,” spokesperson Danielle Alvarez said. “The facts are indisputable: the Chief of Staff had absolutely nothing to do with booking or authorizing any interview.”

A White House official did not respond to The Sun’s question about what the review would involve, or whether it could entail credential or pool changes.

During an Oval Office event Tuesday that included Trump and Vice President JD Vance, Andrew Feinberg, The Independent’s White House correspondent, asked why anyone would use the new government fraud tip line when an 1863 statute already pays whistleblowers a share of what the government recovers.

Vance called the question dishonest, saying the initiative covers more than the False Claims Act. Trump asked Feinberg who he was with. Later, Trump pointed at him: “I don’t know who the hell you are, but you better be careful.” When Feinberg tried to ask a question later, Trump asked, “What’s wrong with you, are you a sick person?” and added, “I actually think there’s something wrong with you.” Vance later called Feinberg an “imbecile” on X, which Feinberg responded to in a separate post. He published an article the next day detailing the event.

“For doing my job,” Feinberg wrote, “I became the target of Trump and his team.”

On Wednesday evening, the White House Press Office emailed Feinberg to say he would “not be the print pooler” for Trump’s Iowa rally, The Independent reported. Feinberg confirmed the removal to The Washington Sun but declined to comment further.

“The White House Correspondents’ Association strongly objects to the decision to restrict a journalist’s coverage simply because the president didn’t care for their questioning. That is retaliation,” WHCA President Jacqui Heinrich said Wednesday on X. “The American public’s right to an independent press depends on reporters being able to do their jobs without fear that challenging the president will cut off their access.”

Asked who made the decision and whether it extends beyond the single assignment, a White House official did not address Feinberg specifically, saying that “no person and no journalist has a constitutional right to access the President’s Oval Office, Air Force One, or other sensitive and private facilities.”

As Trump departed for a South Carolina rally on Wednesday, he turned his frustration on two more reporters. CNN’s Kaitlan Collins pressed him on his decision to waive Russia sanctions he had signed into law last month and on whether the release of U.S. citizen Stephen Hubbard amounted to an exchange.

“You don’t know what you’re talking about,” he told her. “You’re a low-IQ person, you’re a dummy, and you work for CNN.”

Minutes later, ABC News’ Karen Travers asked a version of the same question to him. He responded, “Are you a stupid person? Who do you work for?” Regarding ABC News, he said: “And by the way, your network is the worst of all.”

A CNN spokesperson defended Collins, calling her “an exceptional journalist, reporting every day from the White House and the field with real depth and tenacity.”

The network is pressing a broader complaint. In an Oct. 19 letter to the Justice Department reviewed by The Sun, Boutrous — who represents CNN in addition to Politico — wrote that the White House appears to be implementing “a new unstated policy” barring CNN from the Oval Office and Air Force One and demanded written confirmation by 5 p.m. Thursday that it would stop. Absent that, CNN “will be forced to pursue additional judicial relief.”

CNN has been denied a seat on Air Force One when scheduled to have one since Sept. 18. Those incidents — at least four, per the letter — included the president’s Oct. 16 trip to Georgia and Florida, which came three days after the injunction. The White House has provided no written notice or explanation, Boutrous wrote, and has never directly told CNN it is excluded.

The letter argues the exclusions matter because of where the president now takes questions. He appeared in the White House briefing room twice in 2025, taking about 51 questions, while fielding nearly 2,000 in the Oval Office. Of the roughly 5,000 questions he has answered this term, 97% came there or around Air Force One, the letter said.

Asked about the pool exclusions, a White House official said that Trump “is by far the most transparent President in history, as demonstrated by his many open press gaggles and long White House events this week.”

Then there is the building itself. The New York Times reported Tuesday that Trump is increasingly pushing aides to move reporters out of the James S. Brady Press Briefing Room and has thought about replacing it with an indoor swimming pool. (The room sits atop a pool built for Franklin D. Roosevelt in 1933, which Richard Nixon covered in 1970.)

Asked whether a relocation is under consideration and whether journalists would retain the same access to the West Wing, White House communications director Steven Cheung did not dispute the Times’ account.

“America is rightly distrustful of the Fake News Media because they fabricate stories based off lies and sources who are not even privy to any type of information,” he said in a statement to The Sun. “All options remain on the table and we will make an announcement when appropriate.”

Federal Communications Commission Chair Brendan Carr added a warning of his own Wednesday, saying in a post on X that “broadcasters are prohibited by the terms of their federal licenses from engaging in News Distortion or promoting Broadcast Hoaxes” amid what he called “Fake Polls and Suppression Polls.”

The post did not name any outlets, but followed Wedgewood Polls’ acknowledgement Tuesday that nearly all of its midterm surveys were fabricated. The New York Times pulled 15 of them from its tracking pages later that night.

Anna Gomez, the FCC’s only Democratic commissioner, objected. “FCC rules on news distortion or hoaxes do not apply to a station that reports this data in good faith,” she wrote on X.

Boutrous’ letter about CNN says that a day after the injunction, the White House issued a statement indicative of its bottom line: “The Fake News has no place demanding a spot in the President’s Oval Office.”

entries.title: The Washington Sun Metro: Retrying Times
entries.content:
Good morning. This is The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for Oct. 23, 2026. You can get it in your inbox every day by signing up here — it’s free!

In today’s newsletter: Trayon White, downtown housing and the wrong Washington. 

Capital Weather’s Daily Digit — 8/10. Another sunny, dry day, though a bit cooler and breezy. Highs around 60 to the mid-60s feel brisk in the shade. Read the full forecast.



THE LATEST

D.C. Council member Trayon White’s already-lengthy legal saga just got extended. 

Federal prosecutors said in court Thursday that they intend to seek a new indictment from a grand jury — which could include new charges against the lawmaker — and then proceed with a new trial. Attorneys for White, whose first bribery trial ended in a mistrial last month, argue that prosecutors are unfairly targeting him because of his race and seeking to drive him from elected office, The Washington Sun’s Jenny Gathright reports.

“This is designed to break the back of Mr. White’s efforts to effectively defend himself,” said defense attorney Gary Kohlman, who said it may be prohibitively expensive for White to maintain his current legal team through the duration of a new trial.

U.S. Attorney for D.C. Jeanine Pirro called Kohlman’s statement about racial bias “absurd.”

If there is another trial, it won’t start until May at the earliest, prosecutors said.





DEEP DIVE

D.C. needs more housing, stat. Developers struggling to finance projects are finding hard-won success with a government tax abatement program — dubbed “Housing in Downtown” — that incentivizes them to convert vacant office space into residences.

It’s a rare bright spot in D.C. development news (national lenders apparently see the District as “a serious red flag”), and it’s one that could transform downtown neighborhoods like Dupont Circle, West End and Golden Triangle that never fully recovered after offices bottomed out during the COVID-19 pandemic, The Sun’s Zara Norman reports.

“Our office vacancy [rate] has stabilized, and it’s because we are taking empty offices offline and putting them to new uses,” said Nina Albert, deputy mayor for planning and economic development, at the grand opening of the first project to use the program.

Albert told The Sun that D.C. is on target to bring 15,000 residents to 10,000 downtown units by 2028. Developers say the program could be one way out of the housing crisis, which one said has placed a “pretty substantial” portion of D.C.’s affordable housing at risk of failure.

“The affordable housing crisis that we’re having right now, I hope, is a temporary problem that we’re continuing to work on making fixes to, so that we can stabilize that portion of the market and get it back on track,” Albert said.





FROM THE DISTRICT

Rep. Joyce Beatty requested that a federal judge force the Trump administration to reveal communications about the president’s management of the Kennedy Center, The Sun’s Torrie Herrington reports.

A Tuesday court filing claims that the administration improperly withheld information about President Donald Trump’s role in closing the performing arts center for two years, and that Trump’s communications with Kennedy Center staff fall outside the scope of presidential privilege.

Workers could start constructing Trump’s triumphal arch in two weeks, pending final approval from a federal commission stacked with Trump appointees, The Sun’s Kendall Staton reports.





FROM VIRGINIA

Federal authorities arrested state Sen. L. Louise Lucas yesterday in a sprawling public corruption case that includes fraud and racketeering accusations involving a cannabis business she co-owns, The Sun’s Michelle Del Rey reports. The 82-year-old Democrat, who denies the allegations, was a prominent figure behind her party’s redistricting efforts earlier this year.

Democratic Gov. Abigail Spanberger criticized the timing of the arrest so close to an election, and said Lucas and her family “deserve the opportunity to present their defense and speak to the allegations presented.”

Pulling the plug: Amazon will not build data centers on George Washington University’s Ashburn campus after facing local backlash, The Washington Post reports.

Washington Manassas Airport officials celebrated breaking ground on a new $41 million air traffic control tower, a project the director said was 26 years in the making, according to a news release. The new tower will replace the current one the city bought from a Colorado airport in 1992 for $65,000. The city expects to complete construction by 2029.





FROM MARYLAND

Seven schools in Montgomery County were placed under “secure” status following a shooting near Walter Johnson High School on Wednesday, FOX 5 reports.

After reviewing surveillance camera footage, authorities concluded that the four individuals they detained in relation to the shooting were victims and that they had not identified a suspect, the department said in a news release.





METRO MOMENT

Caps sweatshirt screenshot (1284x2196, AR: 0.58)
Thanks to Reddit sleuths, we know that, as recently as Wednesday night, Fanatics was selling a Capitals sweatshirt that featured the outline of Washington ... state.

The problem is that the Capitals play in Washington, D.C., not in the Pacific Northwest — a fact that can be verified in a number of places, including Google. The link for the sweatshirt, which was for women and retailing at $64.99, now leads to a more general page on the Fanatics website. In other words: The sweatshirt is no longer for sale, officially making it a limited-edition item.

It is not the first time, either, that a clothing company has mixed up the District and Washington state in apparel for a D.C. team. Geography’s hard, after all, and there are just so many professional franchises to keep straight.





SPORTS

The Wizards’ season-opening win on Wednesday marked a turning point for the franchise, The Sun’s Dave Sheinin writes. After three years of misery, Washington finally seems committed to winning and they just might have the talent to do so. Star forward Anthony Davis, who was dominant in the win over Milwaukee, said it wasn’t hard to notice the change inside Capital One Arena on Wednesday night.

“The crowd was great. They were into it,” Davis said. “Last year … it was like ‘Dress Like a Seat Night’ in here.”

Capitals center Pierre-Luc Dubois has missed the past five games with an illness, but Washington got some good news Wednesday as the veteran suited up for practice. There is no official timeline for his return, but The Sun’s Emma Baccellieri writes that Dubois should provide a “dynamic, meaningful boost” when he does get back out on the ice.

At Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology in Alexandria, a unique football program is led by a trailblazing coach. When she was hired this offseason, Rachel Worsham became the first female varsity football coach in Virginia, and at T.J. she faces a distinct challenge. Representing one of the best public magnet schools in the country, many Colonials are playing football for the first time. The Sun’s Noah Ferguson profiles Worsham and her team.

What to Watch This Weekend

Friday

NBA: Wizards vs. Raptors, 7 p.m. (Monumental)

Saturday

MLS: D.C. United vs. Cincinnati, 7:30 p.m. (Apple TV)

NBA: Wizards at Bulls, 8 p.m. (Monumental)

Sunday

NWSL: Spirit at Kansas City Current, 5 p.m. (ESPN)

NFL: Chiefs at Seahawks, 8:20 p.m. (NBC)

entries.title: Morning Sun: Press-ure
entries.content:
Today’s notice: The White House takes a W in its war on the press. A whip around the midterm map. A scoop about Mayor Pete’s schedule. Epstein features prominently in Democratic ads. Not trusting mail-in ballots. And: The State Department has more to say.





THE LATEST

White House media-war victory lap: In Susie Wiles-gate, the score is officially Donald Trump 1, Press 0. That’s how the White House sees it. Politico all but retracted a story about the White House chief of staff and the five-day press secretary, Katie Zacharia, yesterday, after the piece drew anger — and threats — from the White House. Other Politico reporting around Wiles that Trump was also mad about stands unchanged, and in reality, this whole thing is about whether Wiles directly made a TV interview happen or just said it was a great idea for the interview to happen.

“Politico showed their entire ass to the world and played themselves,” a White House official told The Washington Sun’s Jasmine Wright.

It should not be overlooked that in this whole affair — as in many others — this White House has taken a, shall we say, constitutionally sketchy position on press freedom. The Sun’s Ayah Ali-Ahmad details all the recent threats, bans and legal actions flung from this administration at many outlets. In the case of Politico, the White House counsel’s office sent a letter to the publication this week demanding the retraction and removal of three articles about Wiles. The outlet’s lawyer responded that Politico “determined it was appropriate to correct one of the three articles identified in your letter.”

Politico declined to respond to the White House victory lap but pointed to that letter its lawyer sent the counsel’s office saying the outlet “categorically rejects the false accusations” against it.

More: DOJ Investigating Corey Lewandowski Over Alleged Contract Misconduct At DHS: Reports • Supreme Court Rules New Hampshire Can Limit Student ID Use for Voting • Veterans Ask Judge to Block Construction of Trump’s Triumphal Arch





THE MAP


Georgia: Conservative disarray. Prominent right-wing pundit Erick Erickson wrote yesterday that he won’t vote for the Republican nominee for Senate, Mike Collins, and plans to leave the ballot line blank. “I am simply done eating the shit sandwich,” Erickson wrote.

Michigan: Democrats say they’re losing. A small-dollar fundraising email from Democrat Abdul El-Sayed yesterday blared “Rogers pulled ahead” in the subject line, referring to Mike Rogers, the Republican nominee for Senate. “A new poll dropped showing Rogers up by 2 points,” the email reads, before asking for $10.

Ohio: The age factor. The Sun’s Paul Kane reports from Perrysburg, where Democratic Senate nominee Sherrod Brown, who’s 73, will be on the ballot with 9th District Democratic Rep. Marcy Kaptur, who is 80. Derek Merrin, Kaptur’s Republican opponent, likes to point out that he wasn’t born when she first took office in 1983, and many of the ads against both Brown and Kaptur focus on their years in office. “They try to say, you know, she served there too long,” Kaptur told Paul. “Oh no, it took me four decades to get where I am now.”

Alaska: Loosely defined independent? We report from Anchorage, where fisherman and former public school official Bill Hill is running without a party for the state’s lone House seat. His opponent is not buying it: “When you see a candidate that is endorsed by the Democrats, funded by the Democrats, funded by Democrat super PACs, endorsed by Democrats in Congress, it’s obvious which side of the aisle he’s aligned himself with,” Republican Rep. Nick Begich told The Sun’s Alex Roarty.

Texas: Dummymander alert! Trump yesterday switched a planned visit to Waco this weekend to Corpus Christi, which “will bring him closer to some of the state’s most competitive congressional contests,” conservative outlet Texas Scorecard reports. Corpus Christi was drawn into the 34th District by Texas Republicans last year to make a district that already voted for Trump even more pro-Trump.

Meanwhile, things are getting pretty chippy down the stretch in this state. Sarah Stogner, a Republican district attorney in West Texas, told The Sun’s Daniella Diaz she’s launching an investigation into mysterious trans-themed mailers she’s said are a bid to agitate voters ahead of the midterms.

California: HRC spends against Pelosi’s replacement pick. The retiring former speaker has endorsed San Francisco supervisor Connie Chan in the Democrat-vs.-Democrat general election for the 11th Congressional District. Human Rights Campaign’s PAC went up yesterday with $1 million for Chan’s opponent, state Sen. Scott Wiener, a longtime LGBTQ+ rights advocate.

FROM THE CAMPAIGN TRAIL


First on The Sun: Pete Buttigieg’s final sprint. The last 10 days of the midterms will see Buttigieg make three stops in his adopted home state of Michigan, while also rallying in states with competitive Senate races like Georgia, Mississippi and Minnesota, The Sun’s Alex Roarty reports.

The Epstein election: When Democrats want to make inroads in red places in 2026, more often than not they do it with a slew of TV ads featuring Jeffrey Epstein, The Sun’s Avani Kalra reports. More than 150 ads centered on Epstein have aired across the country during the 2026 election cycle, and they began playing primarily in “toss-up” districts and states — but increasingly are being deployed in those Trump won in 2024.

People don’t want to vote by mail. Or rather, not as much. Natalie Fertig reports for The Sun on the initial trends from this year’s early-voting numbers. In Ohio, absentee ballot requests this year have decreased by about 28%, while early in-person voting has increased by about 196% compared to 2022. Similar things are happening in other states. Experts, election officials and Democratic voters tell Natalie that Trump’s attempts to control mail-in balloting has had an effect on people’s trust in the system.





NEW ON THE WASHINGTON SUN

Our State scoop is still going: The Sun’s Eric Katz reported this week on Foreign Service officers up for promotion at the State Department being asked who they voted for in recent presidential elections. Seven hours after our story was published, the State Department issued an addendum to its previous comment to “reject this absurd premise that individuals are being asked about their political affiliations, and even more so for promotions.”

“This Administration will prioritize merit rather than giving out leadership positions based on the number of years individuals have been at the Department,” a department spokesperson said in the new statement. Eric reported that after publication, he heard from more people familiar with the line of questions in question.



More: ICE Extends Contract for Company After Delayed Detainee Medical Payments • Trump-Linked Crypto Company Accused of ‘Public Corruption’ in New Lawsuit





NOT US

  • The Art of the Deal: Jared Kushner’s Hacked Phone Revealed His Secret Negotiations, by Matthew Cole for Vanity Fair
  • Putin Nears a Prize: Restoring Ties With the U.S. While Giving Up Nothing, by Valerie Hopkins for The New York Times
  • Ballot Rejections Soared in Rural Counties After USPS Reduced Mail Service, by Ken B. Morales, Jen Fifield and Misty Harris for ProPublica

entries.title: Democrats Are Losing Trust in Mail-In Ballots
entries.summary: Some voters say they’re worried that Trump might use the USPS to interfere in the election.
entries.content:
Brian Bronzynski doesn’t usually vote early, but he was the first person in line to do so in his rural Iowa precinct on the day early voting began.

Bronzynski, a registered Democrat and retired special education teacher, said he typically votes by mail or in person closer to Election Day. But this year, he is one of the many Democrats rushing to the ballot box early as trust in the U.S. Postal Service is in steep decline.

“I'm not gonna even give them the chance to screw up my ballot and not get it to me in time that I can get it taken care of and get it sent back in. I'm just going to go up there and do it,” he said. “I was also afraid that if I showed up on Election Day, I was going to walk in there and [they’d] say, ‘Oh, we don't have you registered.’”

Trust in the USPS to deliver mail-in ballots on time, which has been steadily growing less reliable over recent years, dropped precipitously this year after President Donald Trump issued an executive order in March prohibiting the agency from delivering mail-in ballots to voters who were not on preapproved voter lists.

The Supreme Court eventually blocked the order. But the administration has continued to raise alarm over mail-in ballots. In September, a whistleblower said USPS was rushing “untested” technology ahead of the midterms that could “derail” the election.

“It further raised concerns, especially from Democrats, that the Postal Service was no longer a trusted authority, that it didn't have the resources to do what it used to do in terms of delivering mail and that it was increasingly under the control of the Trump administration and might intentionally not deliver ballots in some cases,” said Barry Burden, a professor of political science at the University of Wisconsin–Madison who studies voting.

Democrats have staunchly defended broad mail-in ballot use over the last few years as the practice became more politicized. Republicans were once strong supporters of mail-in ballots. But during the pandemic, as mail-in voting increased, Trump and other conservative figures claimed that mail-in ballots were rife with fraud, decreasing trust in the practice among Republican voters.

Concerned Democrats say their worries over mail-in ballots differ sharply from those of Republicans.

“There's no fraud” in mail-in voting, Ohio state Rep. Tristan Rader (D) argued. “It's more that [Republicans are] moving the goalposts. They're making it harder for people to count their votes.”

Burden says the behavior shifts may be seen the most in states where mail-in ballots are growing in use but not yet universal, and states that have a hard Election Day delivery deadline.

Early voting data in some states is already showing that shift. In Ohio, for example, the total number of ballots as of Tuesday was about 30,000 higher than at the same point in the 2022 election, according to the Ohio Secretary of State.

But when and how Ohioans are voting has shifted dramatically: Absentee ballot requests this year have decreased by about 28%, while early in-person voting has increased by about 196% compared to 2022.

Nearly 2,000 people voted on the first day of early voting in Cuyahoga County, one of Ohio’s most populous counties and the home of Cleveland. That’s a 250% increase from previous years.

Ohio’s mail-in ballot law now requires that ballots arrive by Election Day. Previously, they just needed to be postmarked by Election Day.

“The national discourse has had an absolutely huge impact on how people feel about [this], and it's showing up in the numbers,” said Rader, who joined the crowds to vote on opening day.

Rader said the crowd was excited and highly motivated to vote, but he has also heard a lot of fears from Ohioans that USPS may not get their ballot in on time.

“People understand that if you show up, your vote will still be fully counted,” Rader said. “Whereas they're not sure anymore that if they vote by mail, their vote's going to 100% be counted.”

In Michigan, 30% more absentee ballots were returned in 2026 a month out from election day than in 2022, per Secretary of State data.

And in Iowa, Democrats have requested fewer absentee ballots than in 2022 and are currently returning them in much higher numbers to county offices or opting to vote in person at the county office or at satellite polling locations, reported Bleeding Heartland, an independent blog focused on Iowa politics.

“People might not be able to tell you all of the details with Trump's executive order and whatever was going on with the courts, but they know that the Trump administration is trying to do something funny with mail ballots,” said Laura Belin, the primary author of Bleeding Heartland. “Whether that's warranted or not, that is definitely a fear I've heard anecdotally from a lot of Democrats.”

The Democratic ground game in Iowa is not pushing vote-by-mail to the extent they have in the past, Belin said, but voters are still being urged to get their ballot in early.

Whether this is a permanent shift in Democratic voting behavior remains to be seen.

“The real super excellent analysis of this will have to be sort of after the election,” said John Forteir, an expert in voting at the American Enterprise Institute. “I doubt it's a very substantive change.”

Bronzynski said that once Trump is out of office, he plans to return to his normal practice of voting by mail or showing up in person closer to Election Day.

“As soon as this hellish period passes,” he said. “I think it will go back to normal as it should.”

entries.title: Pete Buttigieg Is Staging an Aggressive Final Midterms Sprint
entries.summary: The potential future presidential candidate is ending this election run with a seven-state tour.
entries.content:
Pete Buttigieg will embark on an aggressive seven-state campaign tour in the final 10 days of the midterm election, according to a copy of his schedule shared with The Washington Sun, as the potential future presidential candidate attempts to boost Democrats in battleground states and districts.

His tour will see him make three stops in his adopted home state of Michigan, while also rallying in states with competitive Senate races like Georgia, Mississippi and Minnesota. He’ll make his final appearance in Detroit on Election Day, trying to rally voters ahead of Michigan’s key Senate race.

The final sprint of events caps a busy year of campaigning, which has seen the former presidential candidate hold more than 50 events with Democratic candidates up and down the ballot.

If he chooses to run, Buttigieg is one of the early leaders for his party’s presidential nomination in 2028, according to polls. He’s widely viewed as all-but-certain to enter the race, although he has publicly demurred when asked about it.



Buttigieg advisers this year have touted the former mayor’s ability to campaign in even red states and districts, saying it’s proof of his popularity with moderate voters. He’ll continue that battleground push on Saturday, campaigning with Democratic Sen. Jon Ossoff in Georgia before campaigning with the Democratic candidate Pia Dandiya in Florida’s 22nd Congressional District on Monday.

According to his schedule, he’ll be in Mississippi on Tuesday with Scott Colom, the Democratic nominee for Senate; Colorado on Wednesday; and Michigan on Thursday and Friday. He will end his trip with visits to Minnesota next Sunday — campaigning with Democratic gubernatorial nominee Amy Klobuchar and Senate nominee Peggy Flanagan — and Wisconsin on Monday, before making his final stop in Detroit.

entries.title: How Independent Are This Year’s Independent Candidates?
entries.summary: The answer could sway House and Senate seats across the country.
entries.content:
ANCHORAGE, Alaska — Bill Hill says he’s a natural-born political independent. His parents? Nonpartisan. He’s spent his party-free career as a fisherman, business owner and educator. He’s now running as an independent for Alaska’s at-large House seat, pledging to work with either party — and defy any ideology — to do what’s best for the state.

He also has been endorsed by the Alaska Democratic Party, is formally backed by the Democratic Congressional Campaign Committee in Washington and has the support of nearly every rank-and-file liberal voter in the state. Republicans are relentlessly attacking his credibility as a true independent, labeling him as nothing more than a Democrat in disguise.

Democrats endorsed Hill after the leading Democratic candidate in the race, Matt Schultz, suspended his campaign and backed the independent, citing his own poor fundraising. But an adviser to Schultz in Alaska, independent political consultant Jim Lottsfeldt, told The Washington Sun in an interview that DCCC officials in Washington had been pressuring Schultz to leave the race for months.

They hoped to clear a path for Hill, Lottsfeldt said, even if he wasn’t running as a Democrat.

A spokesperson for the DCCC did not respond to a request for comment.

“When you see a candidate that is endorsed by the Democrats, funded by the Democrats, funded by Democrat super PACs, endorsed by Democrats in Congress, it's obvious which side of the aisle he's aligned himself with,” Republican Rep. Nick Begich, Hill’s opponent, told The Sun in an interview.

This dispute over what makes a true independent is simmering across the country this election cycle.

A host of independents are in a battle to prove they are not merely off-label Democrats. They argue that they represent a genuinely different political viewpoint, even if many of them do have some ties to the Democratic Party.

In Senate races alone, there’s Seth Bodnar in Montana, Brian Bengs in South Dakota, Todd Achilles in Idaho and Dan Osborn in Nebraska, all trying to beat Republicans through independent campaigns.

Osborn, who ran unsuccessfully against Sen. Deb Fischer in 2024, may have the best shot of any independent Senate candidate this year. He told The Sun that voters are really just looking for permission to break away from the two-party system.

"They will have spent $75 million by the end of this, at least, just calling me a Democrat,” Osborn said of Republicans. “Trying to emerge outside of that message certainly is difficult.”

The fight over these independent candidates could have a significant effect on the outcome of next month’s midterm elections in a political environment that polls indicate is sharply hostile to the GOP. Independents are running mostly in red states, where the Democratic Party is deeply unpopular, and proving to voters that they have a truly independent mindset is probably necessary for them to have any chance of winning.

In Alaska, Hill is running competitively against Begich, according to polls, threatening to win a seat GOP political operatives considered safely Republican when the election cycle began.

Hill defended his independent credentials in his interview with The Sun, saying he holds both progressive and conservative beliefs rooted in a lifetime of experience living and working with all kinds of different people in Alaska.

“I've lived a life in a coastal fishing community that's very conservative in nature. And I've lived a life within education — and it's very progressive,” he said. “I've got great friends across the political map. I've done things in my life, built things in my life, by building coalitions of people from across a political spectrum.”
AP26288108146340 (5184x3888, AR: 1.33)Hill said he supports both abortion and gun rights and has voted for Republicans and Democrats in the past, singling out Republican former Alaska Gov. Jay Hammond for praise. And he dismissed criticism about his record — Begich and allies have focused attacks on prior donations Hill made to Sen. Bernie Sanders and his stand on transgender issues — as disconnected from what most Alaska voters care about.

“They don't want to step up and talk about the things that Alaskans want to hear about,” he said of his critics. “I've traveled all over the state, and Alaskans want a response that talks about the way that the decisions being made in Washington, D.C., is impacting their lives every day.”

Hill has become the Democrats’ de-facto candidate in the race, even receiving formal backing from the Alaska Democratic Party in August. He is part of the DCCC’s “Red to Blue” program, which encourages donors to support candidates who it believes have a chance to flip a Republican-held seat.

“He's been pretty clear that he wants endorsements from a wide range of Alaskans, so he wanted our endorsement,” Eric Croft, chair of the Alaska Democratic Party, said in an interview.

Lottsfeldt, the independent political strategist, said he was ambivalent about the wisdom of Hill running as an independent. He pointed to the Democratic candidate for Senate in the state, Mary Peltola, as proof that Democrats can run successfully in Alaska as long as they differentiate themselves from the national party.

“Why are you trying to hide it?” he said. “Don't be disingenuous with me. Just tell me who you are. I'll accept it.”

Lottsfeldt said he received calls from DCCC officials over the first six months of the year asking if he could persuade Schultz to drop out of the race, with the operatives continually making the point that Hill was raising more money. But he said things came to a head in July, just weeks before the state’s nonpartisan primary, when Democrats were facing the prospect of a split between candidates who appeal to progressive voters. (In Alaska's primaries, the top four candidates regardless of party advance to the general election.)

“They were like, ‘OK, this is the horse we need to ride,’” Lottsfeldt said. “It wasn't unreasonable, particularly if you're thinking, ‘Well, they're both the same.’”

Lottsfeldt said he eventually sat down with Schultz to lay out his options, and the candidate dropped out shortly thereafter.

Democratic candidates have pulled out of their races in other states as well. After the Democratic candidate dropped out of Nebraska’s Senate race in July, the state party voted to not fill the vacancy on the ballot, which left a one-on-one race between Osborn and Republican Sen. Pete Ricketts.

In South Dakota, Democrat Julian Beaudion dropped out of the Senate race after facing pressure to step aside to clear the field for Bengs.

Montana didn’t go that way. Alani Bankhead, the Democratic Senate candidate, refused to drop out to make way for Bodnar, even after party leaders urged her to do so. Montana Democratic Party Chair Shannon O’Brien stepped down last week and endorsed Bodnar.

Jane Kleeb, the Nebraska Democratic Party chair, told The Sun that Osborn gives Democrats the best opportunity to get Ricketts out of the Senate because he appeals to more people than a Democratic candidate would.

“He’s not a typical suit-and-tie guy,” she said. “Especially this election cycle, Republicans are looking for candidates who are speaking to them, because MAGA has turned their back on them.”

Unaffiliated candidates have always been a feature of U.S. politics, and Sanders remains the most prominent example. But this year’s cohort of independents is doing something different: Many, including Osborn, have said they would refuse to caucus with either party if elected.

“In fact, we'll caucus with everybody,” he said at an October press conference with other independent candidates. “To do anything else would be a slap in the face to the people of Nebraska.”

Osborn has at times struggled to walk the line between being a true independent and a Democratic-endorsed independent, especially after an audio leak where he criticized Trump voters and called the border wall “a symbol of racism.”

Republicans have jumped at the chance to discredit candidates like Osborn as “fake independents” who would run to caucus with Democrats if elected.

“When you’re recruited by Democrats, funded by Democrats, and parroting Democratic talking points, you’re a Democrat,” said Bernadette Breslin, spokesperson for the National Republican Senatorial Committee, in a statement. “Voters will see through Osborn, Bengs, Achilles, and Bodnar’s fake independent circus this November and reject their radical agenda.”

That messaging has been difficult to escape, Osborn told The Sun.

“If you want to label me, label me as a Teddy Roosevelt Republican, because that's what we're trying to do,” Osborn said. “We're trying to break up the titans of industry to create an economy that favors competition, that elevates the middle class and workers.”

entries.title: In Ohio, Brown and Kaptur Supporters Want ‘Fighting Blood,’ Not ‘New Blood’
entries.summary: Sherrod Brown and Marcy Kaptur bet their decades of populism can outrun calls for new leadership.
entries.content:
PERRYSBURG, Ohio — When Sherrod Brown and Marcy Kaptur first shared a political ticket, in 1982, they were well ahead of their time in the Democratic Party.

Brown, who won Ohio's secretary of state office that year, and Kaptur, who won her first term in Congress, preached an aggressive economic populist message meant to appeal to the working class people who worked in steel mills and auto plants, the type of agenda that fell out of favor during the Clinton and Obama administrations.

Now, after they lost every bit of power in 2024, many Democrats are embracing the Brown-Kaptur message as the future of the party — and yet the other big political force of the moment, an anti-Washington fervor, could doom two Democrats with more than 75 years of combined service in Congress.

Brown and Kaptur used a packed carpenters hall last weekend to say that their experience walking the walk with Ohio’s working men and women is more important than their age.

“No one in Washington, with the exception of Marcy and a few of us, are standing up to the corporations that game the system. But politicians who are supposed to work for you too often work for themselves,” the soon-to-be-74-year-old Brown told a few hundred union members.

In a midterm election where the economy and cost of living is far and away the most important issue, no pair of Democrats seems better positioned to tap into an electorate that is angry at billionaires and the political class. Their mission may have found its moment.

Brown is trying to reclaim a Senate seat after his loss to Bernie Moreno two years ago. Kaptur, 80, is trying to secure her 23rd term in the House, the longest-serving woman in the history of Congress, despite repeated gerrymanders that made her Northwest Ohio district more friendly to President Donald Trump.

Yet their very calling card of legitimacy is the thing Republicans are using against them — their decades in politics, especially in Congress. Republicans are using that throughline of longevity on Capitol Hill in just about every attack ad run against the duo.

One super PAC ad starts off with the theme of “it’s time to retire Marcy Kaptur” and goes on to accuse her of voting over the years to raise taxes and allow federal benefits to go to undocumented immigrants. On Thursday the Senate Leadership Fund unveiled its latest ad against Brown that cites votes cast all the way back to the 1970s in the state legislature.

“Sherrod Brown, 50 years in politics, 50 votes to raise your taxes,” the narrator says in the ad, run by the super PAC affiliated with Senate Majority Leader John Thune.

Kaptur’s opponent, former state legislator Derek Merrin, likes to point out how he wasn’t born yet when she first took office and highlights the region’s economic decline over those decades.

“Since 1983 when Marcy Kaptur took office, America's population across the country has increased by approximately 46% — 46%. In Lucas County, the population has decreased by 9% — failure, she's a failure,” Merrin said earlier this month while campaigning alongside House Speaker Mike Johnson (R-Louisiana), at a logistics company that helps the booming data center business.

Both races, which could determine the majority in each chamber of Congress, are considered pure tossups by The Cook Political Report.

Kaptur offers no apologies for her tenure and suggests that her constituents would be worse off without her fighting for them. She is poised to chair a subcommittee that spends almost $60 billion annually on energy and water projects if Democrats claim the majority, a beneficial post for constituents whose local economy is based in the Great Lakes region.

“Now I have some authority, and they try to use it against me in the ads. They try to say, you know, she served there too long. Oh no, it took me four decades to get where I am now, and I'm not giving it up because it's their seniority, not mine,” she said during an interview in Toledo.

Their most fervent supporters agree, as Ohio state Sen. Paula Hicks-Hudson, who represents Toledo, dismissed talk of needing “new blood” at the carpenters hall rally.

“We need fighting blood,” Hicks-Hudson told the hard-hat crowd.

Out in the audience Brayden McClure, 26, a carpenter from Lima, nodded along as he attended his second rally for Brown in recent weeks. “I need better wages and a better pension, and he has promises and he has ideas for our future,” McClure told The Washington Sun.
Ohio Politics 2026 (8479x5652, AR: 1.50)Two years ago he voted for Trump, after supporting Joe Biden in 2020, a prototypical voter almost always landing on the change candidate. He thinks the Iran war was a huge mistake that drains an extra $100 a week on gas costs driving to his jobs, leading him to support Brown and Kaptur this fall.

“I don't think age matters at all,” he said, preferring experience over youthful energy. “You get someone up there that's going to fight for your rights.”

Public polls give Brown a small but durable lead over Sen. Jon Husted, the former lieutenant governor who was appointed early last year by Republican Gov. Mike DeWine.

The winner in November will take over the remaining two years of a Senate term that Vice President JD Vance won in 2022 — setting up the possibility that Brown would have to immediately gear up for a third straight grueling Senate campaign.

Husted is an imperfect vessel to run as the anti-politician, as he has worked his way up the power ladder in Columbus: 10 years in the legislature, eight as secretary of state and six as DeWine’s lieutenant governor.

Both Brown and Kaptur are running against the Republican machine in the state capital as much as they are running against the Trump administration.

Brown’s ads dubbed Husted as the “face of data centers” after the Republican-dominated legislature approved tax incentives to attract the now controversial projects to rural patches of Ohio. The line of attack proved so effective national Republicans leaked a memo calling the issue “an anchor” around Husted, pleading for the industry to mount its own PR campaign.

Yet over almost 90 minutes of speeches at the carpenters rally, no one blasted Husted on the issue. The reason was hanging on a “We Build Industry” banner along the side of the venue, rattling off the things the union builds.

Fourth on the list: data centers.

“We know it's controversial, but we are in favor of them because it puts a lot of our members to work,” Lee Daher, 46, senior representative of the regional union, told The Sun.

Kaptur explained later that she doesn’t support a full moratorium on the controversial projects but wants these tech companies to better negotiate with county and state officials to ensure water and power usage by the behemoths doesn’t surge costs for local residents.

Their closing message is focused on blaming the richest people in the world for the decades-long decline in the region. “No human being in America should be a trillionaire. Nobody, and I say that to Elon Musk because he's helping to put money against me,” Kaptur said.

Later, when Brown spoke, he added that no one should be a billionaire. He uses a Husted line about how the “work ethic is broken” in America to riff on how the senator should look “in the eye” of a crowd of different trade workers he mentioned and “say your work ethic is broken.”

It’s a message that’s found new relevance in a party that spent the 1990s and first 20 years of this century courting suburban professionals, only to see folks like McClure abandon the party.

Ohio swung from being the quintessential battleground in presidential campaigns, to an afterthought where Trump won by 11% in 2024. Part of this drift came from culture war issues that broke religious, gun-owning rural voters away from Democrats, something Kaptur is distancing herself from in this campaign, which is all about economics.

Everywhere Kaptur goes, an aide must have a sheet of paper showing the median household income by congressional district.

Of the 50 wealthiest, 35 are marked blue for a Democratic representative. The back piece of paper, for the poorest districts, is overwhelmingly red, for Republicans.

“The Democratic Party as a whole couldn't understand this. They couldn't,” she said of the past ethos.

Now, other Democrats are trying to catch up to this message. Brown and Kaptur hope that they will be there in Congress in January to explain to others how they rode it to victory — and they’re warning their supporters to hold these new converts to doing more than just talking the talk.

“That's kind of all they do. They don't fight. They don't come to rallies like this. They don't show up at picket lines. They don't talk to management sometimes and get them to accept that there's an organizing drive,” Brown said. “I know Marcy's done this. I've done this.”

entries.title: At an Elite Magnet School, Coach and Football Program Are a Perfect Match
entries.summary: Rachel Worsham is the first female varsity football coach in Virginia history. Her team is just as unique.
entries.content:
A pack of blue-clad teenagers fan out across a turf field in Alexandria, Virginia, eager to begin practice. It’s early October, and after a month of late-summer heat, there is a welcome crisp in the air. At last — football weather.

The Colonials of Thomas Jefferson High School for Science and Technology quickly get to work. They run through blocking and tackling drills, motivated by a game day around the corner. As her players prepare, Rachel Worsham circles the field with a watchful eye.

Earlier this year, Worsham made headlines by becoming the first female varsity football coach in Virginia high school history. At Thomas Jefferson — long considered one of the best public high schools in the country — the position brings unique challenges for a new coach looking to establish a football culture.

“A lot of the kids — I would say half, give or take — have not played football before,” Worsham said. “If they have, it’s been flag football instead of tackle.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Thomas Jefferson pulls top students from across Northern Virginia into specialized programs focused on college preparation. The school’s coursework is rigorous and time-consuming, making athletic dreams all the more difficult to pursue and, as a result, sports turnout low.

Not far from the football field, the school lists each of its state championship victories in black letters on a brick wall. Atop the list is the school’s decorated debate team. The Scholastic Bowl team and honors band are also featured. The football team is not.

The program may lack prestige, but that didn’t stop Worsham from earnestly applying to the job when it opened in the offseason. A lifelong football fanatic, she saw an opportunity to teach the sport she loves to a group of novices. Now in the thick of her first season, she’s doing just that.

Midway through practice, her voice cuts through the air. It’s time for conditioning. The Colonials line up along the sideline and turn to face their coach.

“If anyone doesn’t go 100%, we start over!” she says.

“Yes, coach!” the players respond.

The whistle blows and they sprint up and back across the turf, returning to the white line a little more breathless each time. To Worsham’s delight, nobody is caught in a jog. After three rounds of sprints, the Colonials break for water and their coach scans the sideline with a grin.

“Aren’t you the track guy?” she asks one player, who is panting with his hands on his hips.

“I run short distance!” he protests. They both laugh.

Worsham fell in love with football growing up in the Midwest. While there weren’t any opportunities for her to play the sport growing up, her passion bloomed as she watched NFL and college games on TV. After graduating from Michigan State, she packed her bags and moved to the D.C. area in the early 2000s.

Worsham didn’t know many people upon her arrival to D.C., so she made connections through Michigan State’s alum network. She quickly found herself a spot on the group’s flag football squad. Soon after, a women’s tackle team — the D.C. Divas of the Women’s Football Alliance — recruited her to play on their offensive line.

“The rest is history,” Worsham said with a smile. “They couldn’t get me off the field until I was done, injury-wise.”

Rachel Worsham (1630x1630, AR: 1.00)
Worsham played 12 seasons for the Divas, winning two national championships. In 2024, she was named to the team’s Hall of Fame.

When injuries put an end to her playing days, she pivoted to coaching. She started at the youth level, then moved to high school. She worked as an offensive line coach at Marshall High in Fairfax for six seasons, then spent two more as an assistant head coach and coordinator for Robinson. Last year, she served as Robinson’s girls’ flag football coach.

“I am not a flag football person by heart, because as a lineman we don’t play the game. So I wanted to get back to my tackle roots,” Worsham said. “That’s why I was so excited that this opportunity came up.”

She was officially hired in January, a few months after Thomas Jefferson hired Jennifer Hammond to coach its varsity baseball team.

Since her arrival, Worsham has honed in on teaching the X’s and O’s of the game. That includes basic principles, like where to line up or what constitutes a penalty. In an attempt to relate to her physics-minded student-athletes, she once likened tackling to two magnets attracting one another.

“We had a practice where we taught them how to fall,” Worsham said. “That’s not normally how you want to do it, and you don’t want to teach falling, but hey — we have to fall, we have to get back up and we have to be safe when we do it.”

Rachel Worsham TJ (8256x5504, AR: 1.50)
As the sun starts to set on this Tuesday practice, the Colonials trot out their offensive unit to continue rehearsing their plays for Friday’s game. Luke Brazie leads the charge — he dons a red practice jersey that he’s cropped above his waist, revealing a back plate that displays the phrase: “DO NOT CROSS”.

Brazie, a senior, is one of the few players on the field who has spent four years in the Colonials’ program. He typically plays wide receiver and defensive back, but with the team’s starting quarterback in concussion protocol this week, he’s taken over under center.

Brazie has seen the impact of Worsham’s coaching firsthand, particularly on the inexperienced freshmen and sophomores. The Colonials have picked up fewer procedural penalties as the season has gone on and the special teams unit has gained confidence. Despite some injuries, things are starting to move in the right direction.

It’s a departure from the past, Brazie said, and a glimpse at what the future of the program could look like.

“It’s a definite culture shift … it’s certainly different this year in a good way,” Brazie said. “We’re more prepared, we’re more competent. We don’t have quite as many talented players, so it doesn’t show on the scoreboard yet, but over the course of [the underclassmen]’s development, I truly do expect to see, over the next few years, T.J. become better than it’s been in a long time.”

After falling into an early 0-2 hole, Worsham’s Colonials got their first chance at victory against Manassas Park in mid-September. Behind a strong night from Brazie, Thomas Jefferson took a 14-6 lead deep into the fourth quarter. But Manassas Park responded with a lengthy touchdown drive. All of a sudden, the Colonials were two points away from potentially squandering their first real chance at victory.

On the two-point try, Brazie lined up man-to-man against the Cougars’ top wide receiver. The ball was lobbed their way, and Brazie got his hand on it to seal the victory.

“I knew I would come out with the win,” Brazie said.

That win marked more than one milestone: It was the first time a woman had ever led a boys football team to a varsity win in Virginia, but it was also the first time many of Worsham’s players had ever won a football game, period. And it left them wanting more.

In the final minutes of practice, Worsham brings the team in for a brief huddle. Brazie and his teammates kneel on the turf and stare up at their coach. Not far from the center of the huddle is Sohum Das, a freshman wide receiver and linebacker who is learning the sport at the varsity level.

In a few minutes, both Brazie and Das will leave this field and reenter the hectic world of high-level high school academics — homework and midterms and college futures. Brazie is set on attending a large engineering school next year. Das is gunning for Thomas Jefferson’s pre-med course and is also interested in pursuing mechanical engineering.

But at this moment, as Worsham breaks the huddle one last time to signal the end of practice, they are just football players doing what they love.

“When I become a senior, I want to go 8-0,” Das said. “All wins.”

entries.title: Democrats Aim to Build Red State Momentum With an Epstein Ad Blitz
entries.summary: Operatives hope what had been a swing-district gambit to exploit voters’ anger at the dead sex trafficker can tip GOP races that had seemed safe.
entries.content:
As the limits of where Democrats hope to win in 2026 creep further into reliably red territory, party operatives have been turning more often to a wedge issue that helped Donald Trump win in 2024 — disgraced financier Jeffrey Epstein.

In Kansas, a state that Trump won by more than more than 16 points that is now considered a genuine pick-up opportunity for Democrats, one advertisement slams Republican Sen. Roger Marshall for his September 2025 vote to block the Epstein files release.

“I expected our leaders to hear our stories and actually hold our abusers accountable. They’ve only let us down,” Marina Lacerda, an Epstein victim, tells the camera while a video of Marshall saying Epstein is “not of much interest” to him plays on the screen.

The issue is not new, but Democratic campaign groups are shifting the focus to places like Kansas, flooding the airwaves and social media feeds with spots about Republicans who stood in the way of quickly releasing FBI files about the dead sex trafficker, hoping the issue can tilt such reach contests into the blue column.

More than 150 ads centered on Epstein have aired nationwide during the 2026 election cycle, according to a review by The Washington Sun. They began playing primarily in “toss up” districts and states across the country but increasingly are being deployed in states and districts that Trump won two years ago, often by wide margins.

And Democrats are expected to ramp up their messaging around Epstein in the final stretch before Nov. 3. The Democratic National Committee is planning a flood of Epstein-related ads in red states over the coming days, Axios first reported, targeting Trump’s base on platforms like Fox News and right-wing YouTube channels.

Epstein is a particularly salient issue for Republicans, said Dane Strother, a Democratic strategist, who described Democrats’ messaging around Epstein as “a layup.”

Throughout his 2024 election campaign, Trump campaigned on declassifying the Epstein files, and 82% of self-identified MAGA Republicans supported releasing all files related to the notorious financier, a 2025 Washington Post poll found.

“People feel deceived,” Strother said. “They fully expected these files to be released, and even the hardcore [Republicans] recognize they haven’t all been released. … We’re not talking about taxes, we’re not talking about privatizing schools, we’re talking about protecting children.”

Democrats have already moved that messaging into even deeper red territory. In Mississippi, a Republican stronghold where the Senate race shifted slightly in Democrats’ favor earlier this week, Democrats are targeting Sen. Cindy Hyde-Smith for the same vote as Marshall.

“Senator Hyde-Smith, you voted to protect the sex trafficker who abused me,” Jena-Lisa Jones, another Epstein survivor, says in one spot running there. “If you vote to protect pedophiles, it’s time for Mississippi to pick a new senator.”

Most GOP senators cast the same vote to block the release of the files in September 2025, though both chambers of Congress later passed the Epstein Files Transparency Act in a near-unanimous vote, following mounting public pressure.

In Colorado’s 5th District, a “lean Republican” seat, the family of the late Epstein victim Virginia Giuffre criticize Rep. Jeff Crank in an ad for “refusing to meet” with them following Giuffre’s death last year.

“Our own Congressman Jeff Crank refused to meet with us,” Giuffre’s sister-in-law Amanda Roberts, who lives in the district, says in the ad. “Then, when he had the chance to expose the truth and release the Epstein files, he repeatedly voted to cover them up.”

Recent polling has shown widespread dissatisfaction within the Republican base over the Trump administration’s handling of the files. Only 21% of Republicans said that the administration helped deliver justice in Epstein-related cases, a June Reuters poll found, a number that is at 10% across all Americans polled.

Strother added that in this year’s political cycle, Democrats may only need to flip a small portion of Republican voters to turn the tide in either chamber of Congress. That makes any issue unpopular with the Republican base important to exploit, he said.

“We need the 8% of [MAGA] voters to perhaps vote, in this case, Democratic, and this is an issue that penetrates red,” Strother added.

Republicans are pushing back. They have slammed Democrats for taking money from donors linked to Epstein. Filings released Wednesday revealed tech billionaire Reid Hoffman, who has been repeatedly connected to Epstein, was the top donor to House Majority PAC, the Democrats’ flagship House super PAC, in the last quarter.

One GOP ad that aired Wednesday in Pennsylvania in Rep. Rob Bresnahan’s “toss up” district against Democrat Paige Cognetti highlights the connection.

“Her lying ads are funded by anti-gun radicals and Epstein Associates. Paige Cognetti is basically Kamala Harris without the charisma,” one ad reads, with a picture of Epstein and dollar bills flashing across the screen.

The Democratic campaign group spent about $2.33 million on ads related to Epstein in nine districts, according to data from ad tracking service AdImpact.

"The soulless shills at House Majority PAC want voters outraged over Epstein ties while cashing checks from Reid Hoffman, who actually visited Epstein’s island,” Mike Marinella, a spokesperson for House Republicans campaign arm, said in a statement. “If these shameless Democrat candidates believed the ads HMP is running for them, they would reject its support and condemn Hoffman.”

Still, Strother said that such attacks have only benefited Democrats. His party has consistently led the narrative on the Epstein issue and spotlighting the financier’s unpopularity can only be beneficial, he added.

“Republicans are answering the attack,” Strother said. “When they have to stop and answer an attack, that means they’re not attacking, and Democrats are winning that debate. That’s exactly the debate that Democrats want to have.”

entries.title: A New Lease on Life for D.C.’s Vacant Offices
entries.summary: The success of a program incentivizing office-to-housing conversions is a rare bright spot in D.C. housing development.
entries.content:
It’s not easy to build housing in D.C. right now.

On top of high interest rates and construction costs, national lenders have called the District “a serious red flag” for its rental nonpayment problem — meaning they lack confidence that landlords can collect a return on their investment.

“Financing in Washington, D.C., right now is extremely challenged,” John Means, co-founder of development firm Rooted Communities, told The Washington Sun. “A pretty substantial portion of our affordable housing [is] at risk of failure.”

But in a rare bright spot for D.C. housing news, developers have found a rock to cling to, and one that could totally alter the makeup of the District’s downtown neighborhoods: a tax abatement program that incentivizes the conversion of vacant office space into housing.

Mayor Muriel Bowser rolled out the program, called “Housing in Downtown,” in 2024. Two years later, the first project financed under the program has been completed: the former Air Line Pilots Association headquarters in Dupont Circle, which was converted to 157 residences. The building, known as Aviator House, is already 70% leased.

Developers say the program, which requires 10% of units to be affordable, has been instrumental in pursuing ambitious projects that may not have otherwise penciled out.

“For us, it was a huge value-unlocking tool,” said Katie Hartley, the managing director of National Real Estate Development. “We bought this building in 2000, so we owned it for 24 years as an office, and then did the conversion.”

The abatement provides millions of dollars in long-term operating cost relief, but it also does something less tangible: The city-backed projects signal confidence to investors and beat back what Means called “perceived challenges” facing the District, like rental nonpayment or the rent freeze initiative that may make it onto the 2028 ballot.

“It was a huge help,” said Austin Gabel of Duball Partners, which is converting another Dupont office building into 160 residences. “Especially when you look at the exit value of similar product that is trading hands recently.”

Sign up for The Washington Sun Metro newsletter for essential coverage of the D.C. region.

Another advantage to the projects, particularly as costs continue to climb, is shorter construction timelines. By right, many of these office buildings are already zoned for multifamily residential use.

“Construction started as fast as we could humanly design the work; rarely is that the case,” Gabel said. “We’d be looking at a 19-month versus 30-month schedule.”

There are plenty of challenges that come with converting a building designed for work into one for living. Windows may be fewer than you’d want in a residence, and many in office buildings don’t open. All residences need new heating and cooling systems and could need more stairwells, elevators and bathrooms, said architect Eric Colbert, whose firm designed Aviator House.
Aviator House (2012x1218, AR: 1.65)It takes a lot of creativity to get all those features — particularly ample light and air — into each unit, he said, and all those adaptations can run up costs. Means said he’s seen these projects come out both cheaper and pricier than the average new build, so his firm is choosy about what it pursues.

“Development in any form right now is extremely expensive,” he said. “We're on the feasibility borderline for most projects.”

The abatement program’s goals are bigger than cutting developers a break. Bowser hopes the initiative will bring 15,000 D.C. residents into downtown neighborhoods like Golden Triangle and West End by 2028, in 10,000 units. Nina Albert, the deputy mayor for planning and economic development, told The Sun that the administration is on track to reach that goal.

“We're going to convert blighted or vacant offices to vibrant residences, which keeps our downtown exciting and vibrant,” she told reporters at the opening for Aviator House last week.

Once-bustling offices in downtown D.C. bottomed out during the COVID-19 pandemic, and with the rise of remote work, they never fully recovered. The office vacancy rate in the District was 21.3% by the end of the third quarter of the 2026 fiscal year, according to Colliers. That is nearly double what it was pre-pandemic, but less than a 2024 projection that the vacancy rate would be 27% by 2027.

“Our office vacancy [rate] has stabilized, and it's because we are taking empty offices offline and putting them to new uses,” Albert said at the opening. “What could have, without an intervention or without private investment, been a continuing increase in office vacancy, and that sucking of vibrancy, you’re now introducing new uses that allow District residents to live, work and play here in downtown and enjoy the beauty of our city.”

Bowser plans on “running through the tape” until January, Albert said, when she leaves office and a successor — presumably Democratic nominee Janeese Lewis George — takes the helm. Developers indicated that in a challenging development environment, office-to-housing conversions might be a key tool in reaching Lewis George’s ambitious goal of building 72,000 units in five years.

“The affordable housing crisis that we're having right now, I hope, is a temporary problem that we're continuing to work on making fixes to, so that we can stabilize that portion of the market and get it back on track,” Albert said.

entries.title: Trump Administration Lays Out a Path to Challenge Alaska’s Senate Results
entries.summary: A lawsuit filed this week claims that a candidate who shares the same name as incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan is only running “for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters.”
entries.content:
The federal government sued Alaska elections officials this week as part of an attempt to preemptively line up a challenge to the results should Republican Sen. Dan Sullivan lose his race.

The lawsuit, filed Thursday in the U.S. District Court for the District of Alaska, centers around the claim that a second candidate who shares a name with incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan is only running “for the purpose of confusing or misleading voters and compromising the fairness of the ballot,” according to the filing.

The race is currently one of the most competitive in the country and has the potential to swing the balance of power in Congress’ upper chamber.

The case, filed less than two weeks before Election Day, is before Judge Sharon L. Gleason, an appointee of former President Barack Obama.

The second Dan Sullivan — who will appear as Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. on the ballot — filed to run three days before the filing deadline. The Trump administration’s lawsuit makes the case that if the incumbent Sen. Dan Sullivan loses, an investigation should be carried out determining whether voters were confused about which Sullivan they were voting for before certifying any election results.

“It is vital that Defendants not certify any election result that may be impacted by voter confusion,” lawyers for the Department of Justice wrote in the filing. “An election may be impacted by voter confusion if: (1) Senator Sullivan does not win the election; and (2) had all votes cast for Daniel J. Sullivan been cast instead for Senator Sulivan and Alaska’s ranked-choice process played out accordingly, Senator Sullivan would have won the election.”

Previous efforts by the Alaska Division of Elections and the state Republican Party to prevent the new Sullivan from running against the incumbent senator failed earlier this year when the Alaska Supreme Court ruled that both Sullivans could remain on the ballot.

On Thursday, Attorney General Todd Blanche refused to rule out the possibility that his department would intervene in states’ independent processes for certifying their midterm elections, saying extreme scenarios could prompt federal intervention.

In a Truth Social post earlier this week, President Donald Trump said his administration was looking at “powerful legal options to remove the fraudulent Daniel J. Sullivan Jr. from the ballot.”

“I am very concerned about the Dan S. Sullivan Race for the U.S. Senate in Alaska in that it is totally confusing,” Trump wrote in the post.
