entries.title: Democrats Warn Economy — Not Impeachment — Should Drive Agenda
entries.summary: “Costs are number one, two, three, four and five” on the to-do list, one Democratic operative said.
entries.content:
Democrats are preparing a broad oversight agenda if the party sweeps control of one or both chambers of Congress in the midterm elections, signaling investigations of President Donald Trump, his family, his aides and top Republican donors amid a string of reports of corruption in Washington.

But Democratic operatives are warning lawmakers not to lose sight of what polls show the November election is really about: inflation and the high costs of consumer goods, fuel and health care. Americans are deeply dissatisfied with Trump’s economy — nearly 70% of likely voters disapprove of the president’s handling of the cost of living, according to a New York Times/Siena poll released on Wednesday. This economic discontent has positioned Democrats to flip seats, even in traditionally red areas, in November.

While voters also rank corruption near the top of their list of concerns, it is the bread and butter issues that should be the Democrats’ driving force as they plot an agenda for the next Congress, these operatives told The Washington Sun.

“Costs are number one, two, three, four and five,” said Lanae Erickson, senior vice president at the center-left think tank Third Way. “I would hope that House Democrats keep their eye on that ball.”

“If you’re just going to try to impeach Trump again, or make a big to-do about the fact that Don [Trump] Jr. is making a bunch of money off of defense contracts, which he is, how does that connect back to people's real lives?” Erickson asked. “Corruption alone is not going to do it for voters.”

Democratic strategists noted that voters harbor doubts that their party will actually follow through on their promises to lower costs instead of spending their time on other priorities, like impeaching Trump. The party previously sought to use the partisan and time consuming impeachment process to oust Trump from power in 2019 and 2021, but fell short both times due to Republican opposition in the Senate.

Democratic lawmakers argue this time should be different.

“It might be emotionally satisfying for 10 seconds to impeach the president a third time and then have him be not convicted in the Senate, but I'm not sure what that would get us,” Hawaii Sen. Brian Schatz recently told The Sun.

“Voters want accountability on Trump, but they do worry Democrats will be so focused on Trump that they won’t get anything done that matters in their lives,” added a Democratic strategist who requested anonymity to speak freely. “You can still focus on corruption, but every corruption story has to end with a number on a bill.”

On the campaign trail over the last two weeks, House Minority Leader Hakeem Jeffries has talked up addressing both high costs and corruption, telling voters in Pennsylvania that “we recognize that in addition to fighting for an affordable America, we’ve got to bring accountability to this out of control Trump cartel.”

Rep. Debbie Dingell signaled some things on the Democratic wishlist may take time to accomplish, but they aim to address both priorities. The Michigan Democrat said the party is planning “a 100-hour agenda,” as well as “a 100-day agenda.”

“I think part of the first 100-hour agenda is we’ll need to reverse some of the cuts that have cost people their health care, reverse how we now have hungry children and seniors because of the cuts to Medicaid,” Dingell told The Sun this week. “But at the same time, we’re going to hold corrupt officials accountable, because what they’ve been doing is significantly contributing to increased costs.”

Leaders in both chambers have sketched out in broad strokes their policy agenda next year if voters return them to power. They want to end the war in Iran, roll back Republican cuts to Medicaid and federal food assistance, repeal the president’s global tariffs and extend Obamacare health insurance subsidies that lapsed in 2025.

Whether they can accomplish all that will depend on the size of the Democratic majorities and if they flip control of both the House and Senate. And actually putting these policies into place will be difficult, given that Trump and his veto pen will occupy the White House for the next two years.

The Democratic desire for an ambitious, go-fast agenda might also conflict with Jeffries' support for returning the House to regular order, a legislative process that gives more influence to congressional committees. But those committees would need to be constituted with new members for that process to begin. And priorities like repealing Republican cuts to Medicaid may require more extended negotiations if Democrats plan to find a way to pay for reversing those cuts.

House Democrats have more than one plan to satiate the party’s base’s desires to confront what they argue is the historic corruption of the Trump administration. Rep. Robert Garcia, the California Democrat set to lead the investigative House Oversight Committee if his party wins a majority, has outlined sprawling plans to probe the president, his family and close circle of allies. That includes an expanded panel investigation into convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein and his network of connections, including the president.

Other Democratic targets will likely include the donors funding Trump’s ballroom construction at the White House, the Trump family’s vast crypto holdings and foreign business deals, alleged self-dealing by top Trump officials, high-value foreign gifts given to the president, and Elon Musk’s reported slowdown of Starshield’s satellite network in Ukraine.

“Trump’s foreign policy is focused on turning our government infrastructure into a shakedown operation for the Trump family and his cronies. So we will be relentless in going after that corruption and getting that money back,” Rep. Jason Crow of Colorado told reporters on Wednesday.

Americans’ perceptions of corruption are at their highest level in 20 years, with 89% of U.S. adults saying it is widespread in the government, according to a Gallup survey released last month. Meanwhile, nearly 70% of Americans believe Trump is using the presidency to enrich himself, including one-third of Republican and Republican-leaning independents, according to a recent Washington Post-ABC News-Ipsos poll.

Corruption has been a big theme on the campaign trail this election cycle, with both Democratic and Republican candidates running on transparency, ethics reform and anti-corruption measures. A push to ban lawmakers and their families from trading individual stocks stalled in the Senate this year, but Democrats are likely to try again next year.

“Corruption is an issue that has flipped plenty of seats in the past with unlikely candidates winning,” Connecticut Democratic Sen. Chris Murphy said this week in an interview with MS NOW. “You’ve got a Republican Party that doesn’t seem to know what to say. Trump is offering them no cover. … That’s a real toxic message for Republicans that’s likely going to result in the Senate flipping to Democratic control.”

Erickson cautioned Democrats to avoid votes on a laundry-list of items designed to appease their various constituency groups, such as on abortion, campaign spending and LGBTQ issues, and keep their focus squarely on lowering costs.

“Trump created this opportunity for us, but we absolutely have not yet made the case to voters that we are a credible alternative on a lot of these issues,” Erickson said. “If Democrats win this election based on costs and corruption related to driving up costs, and then start with a quick list of interest group priorities, that is not going to be particularly satisfying.”

entries.title: Hegseth Issues Directive to Stop Soldiers From Betting on Prediction Markets
entries.summary: At least one member of the U.S. military has already been charged for allegedly placing such a wager.
entries.content:
Defense Secretary Pete Hegseth is warning soldiers that they are prohibited from using “nonpublic information” to place bets on online prediction markets, warning that any violation of the rule may result in administrative punishment or even criminal prosecution.

Hegseth’s memo, sent to senior Defense Department personnel on Oct. 2, is an apparent attempt to crack down on a growing problem that has already resulted in charges against at least one member of the U.S. military: 38-year-old Master Sgt. Gannon Ken Van Dyke, who was arrested earlier this year on accusations that he bet close to $33,000 on the Jan. 3 operation to capture ex-Venezuelan leader Nicolás Maduro — an operation that he participated in.

Gannon reportedly made more than $400,000 in profit from the wager.

The memorandum bans betting on classified or unclassified information on “traditional betting platforms” or prediction markets like Kalshi and Polymarket. The document wasfirst reported by CBS.

Hegseth warned in the memorandum that trades made with insider knowledge could create a “signal” that helps foreign actors anticipate military plans or movements.

“Our enemies watch movements in these markets,” Hegseth wrote. “That signal can be aggregated, correlated, and exploited by hostile foreign intelligence services to anticipate our movements, targets, and timing.”

The memorandum also warns members that having financial stakes in the outcomes of their work could warp their judgment and distract them from the department's “sacred mission.”

“That is precisely the kind of dilution of the warrior ethos this Department has strived to eradicate under this administration,” Hegseth wrote. “We are restoring lethality, discipline, and singular focus on fighting and winning our Nation's wars.”
entries.author: Andrea Padilla

entries.title: This Brewers-Rays World Series Is the Brainiac Classic
entries.summary: A viewer's guide to a World Series that features two of baseball's most analytics-minded teams.
entries.content:
In the World Series, starting Friday between Milwaukee and Tampa Bay, many fans will have the same thought in many a crisis moment.

“Why???”

Why on earth are they doing that?

For example, with the Brewers’ 100-RBI star Brice Turang coming to bat with the bases loaded, why might the Rays relieve their ace Drew Rasmussen with 34-year-old journeyman Cam Booser who once retired from baseball for four years to be an acoustical ceiling carpenter?

Are they crazy?

Why would the Brewers be happy if the Rays used as many left-handed hitters in their lineup as possible against Game 1 starter Jacob Misiorowski, even though he is right-handed and has thrown 105 mph?

Shouldn’t right-handed hitters be terrified?

We’ll try here to help explain some of the possible puzzlers in what could be called The Brainiac Classic. The Rays have 39 people in their analytics department, all frying their big brains trying to get any edge. The Brewers have 46 analytics wizards! (They’ve also got 144 scouts between them.) Both of these teams, although small-market, are among the top spenders on baseball science, per MLB Network.

For comparison, the Washington Nationals, whose new regime emphasized such methods in ’26, plan to increase their analytics department from 19 to more than 30 by next season. The bare-bones Baltimore Orioles front office has 12.

The analytics revolution has a hundred manifestations, from the weights you lift to add two miles per hour to your fastball; to a new grip to make your slider travel in a different plane; to the way a hitter divides up the strike zone into “lanes” in search of prime pitches to hit because he knows he can’t “cover” every pitch in every location.

In this fascinating but sometimes paralyzing maze of data, let’s start with just one illustration that shows how small-market teams, like these, create value at all 26 roster spots to battle clubs with two or three times their payroll.

For example, take Booser versus Turang.

Second baseman Turang owns a Platinum Glove as the game’s best fielder at any position. He once stole 50 bases. He can bunt or blast.

Booser was lousy in college, rotten in the minors and even after forsaking acoustical ceilings, was still awful in his comeback with the Amarillo Sod Poodles.

Yet, if they meet, Turang will have very little chance. At least in Analytics World.

Why?

Last winter, Tampa Bay got Booser for nothing and sent him to their Rays pitching lab. They overhauled his pitch usage and modified the shapes of his secondary pitches. He tripled the use of his redesigned cutter — from 20% to 60% in the first two pitches of at-bats, when modern hitters tend to hunt fastballs. The new cutters made his decent mid-90s fastball look faster. Once ahead, he erased hitters, especially lefties, with breaking stuff.

Thus reinvented, Booser ate AAA alive with a 1.80 ERA. In 43 games as a Ray, his ERA was 1.98. Lefties batted .123 and slugged .323, which would be bad if a pitcher tried to hit. In six games this postseason, his ERA is 0.00.

Not bad for a guy who, before he retired in ’17, had endured a broken femur, Tommy John surgery, a torn labrum and being hit by a car.

Turang, on the other hand, is a marvelous player but endures the curse of many of the best left-handed hitters in MLB history: He isn’t nearly as good against lefties as against righties.

Neither was Ted Williams, whose OPS was 229 points lower against lefties than righties. His slugging average dropped from .666 (not far from Babe Ruth) to .495 (close to CJ Abrams).

Williams is an extreme case. But Lou Gehrig, as well as contemporaries like Juan Soto, Shohei Ohtani, Bryce Harper, Freddie Freeman and Brewer Jonathan Aranda all have lower career OPS marks by 120 to 160 points.

This season, the gap for Turang was 282 points! He slugged a pathetic .313 against lefties. And that is all lefties, not a specially created Frankenstein like Booser who held lefties to a .123 batting average and .388 slug.

If Turang homers in that matchup, every computer in MLB will explode. (I’ll just smile. As Turang showed by homering off lefty Tarik Skubal in the NLCS, analytics are percentages, not prophecy.)

Throughout history, the average left-handed hitter’s OPS drops by 80 to 90 points against lefties. The average right-hander’s OPS only falls versus righties by about 40 to 50 points.

Why is this? Standard answer: 90% of us are righty. If you’re a righty but can’t learn to hit righties, even though the ball looks like it’s coming near your head, you quit baseball. Many lefties see few lefties on their journey. Less familiarity equals less mastery. Until, oops, 25% of MLB pitchers are lefties.

MLB has known about this handedness-factor since at least 1914 when George Stallings, the manager of the Miracle Braves in Boston, platooned at every outfield spot. Others, like Casey Stengel and Earl Weaver, loved platoons and playing for late-inning matchups.

But these days, finding edges, especially if you are “poor,” is almost a religion, especially in constructing superb bullpens with interlocking, complementary parts like the Rays and Brewers.

Milwaukee’s southpaw DL Hall held lefties to a .173 slug, while righty Abner Uribe negated right-handed slug to .182. Lefty Aaron Ashby and righty Trevor Megill just get everybody out.

The Rays have two bullpen mind-benders whose excellent change-ups and splits — which break away from the bats of opposite-handed hitters — give them “reverse splits.” To make matters more confusing, one of them is a lefty who pitches like a righty (Ian Seymour), and the other is righty closer Bryan Baker, who, statistically, might as well be a lefty.

Who the devil should be your pinch hitter?

The Brewers also have Kevin Kelly — a side-arming righty who knocks 208 OPS points off righties. You can bet the Rays star Jackson Chourio, who hit 201 OPS points lower against righties this year, will see Kelly in a crisis.

In this era, switch-hitters or hitters who have no “handedness” weakness are especially valuable. The current rule that relief pitchers must either face a minimum of three batters or finish an inning forces managers to look for “pockets” in the other lineup where at least two of those “minimum three hitters” are favorable matchups. If a star hitter has no right-left weakness, he’s a pocket-buster.

In that flaw-free category, the Brewers have Jake Bauers and William Contreras. The Rays counter with Junior Caminero and, this year, Yandy Díaz.

Amid all this complexity, sometimes simplicity matters most. The Dodgers’ Max Muncy was asked why his team had so much trouble with the Brewers bullpen. “They all throw 100 with great breaking stuff,” he said.

Got any more dumb questions?

My favorite outlier in this series is the hardest thrower of all: Misiorowski.

The Miz’s fastball appears to rise and also has an elite 11.2-inch arm-side “run.” Combine that with his 6-foot-7 height, his 7-foot-6 stride and his fairly low arm angle and you have a pitch that appears to explode up and away from lefties. After heavy doses of that, his breaking pitches yield high swing-and-miss rates.

Will that Miz, who held lefties to a .114 batting average with no power, be the one we see in this World Series? At 24, he’s never had this many starts before and his fastball’s velocity, rise and run have all ticked down slightly — not much, but measurably in a Statcast era. Is that why so many Padres and Dodgers fouled off so many pitches in his postseason starts, getting him out of the game in the fifth inning both times?

In the NLCS, the Brewer bullpen got more outs than its starters. In this whole post-season, Ashby, Megill and Hall have a 0.00 ERA in 23 1/3 innings. Can the Brewers keep getting perfection by the beer-barrel-ful?

If the Brewers’ (only) three trusted starters, The Miz, Robert Gasser and Logan Henderson, are close to their first-rate regular-season form, then the spirit of Bob Uecker may not rest uneasy for much longer. If they don’t, this could be a long, tight, IQ test of a World Series for anybody who watches it from anywhere.

Even the top row.

entries.title: Trump Shrugs Off the Rape Charges Central to Amy Acton Ad Controversy
entries.summary: The president waved away questions about Amy Acton’s stepfather, who was charged with sexually abusing the candidate when she was a child.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump continued to defend Republican gubernatorial nominee Vivek Ramaswamy’s ad that featured the estranged mother of his Democratic opponent, Amy Acton, telling reporters he didn’t know “anything” about the stepfather who was accused of sexually abusing Acton when she was a child.

“I know that recently a mother got on television and said that her daughter should not be governor of Ohio,” Trump told reporters at the White House on Friday. “And she said, 'I love my daughter, but my daughter lies all the time.’ … This has nothing to do with the stepfather or anything else.”

Ramaswamy’s campaign released a divisive ad on Tuesday featuring Acton’s mother, Donna Arthur, who called her daughter a liar and urged Ohioans not to vote for her.

Acton said the pair has been estranged for more than 40 years: She was removed from her mother’s custody at 12 after her stepfather was arrested and charged with raping Acton. Donna Arthur stayed with the stepfather even after the allegations.

The president told a rally crowd in Iowa on Thursday that Ramawamy had come to him for advice, and that he told the gubernatorial candidate to stand by his message.

“I told him, ‘Leave it up,’” Trump said Thursday. “And look upstairs and say, ‘Thank you, God, very much — I appreciate it!’”

Trump’s interaction with an NBC News reporter who asked about the ad on Friday turned hostile, with the president telling her to be “quiet” and calling her a “horrible little reporter.”

Ramaswamy also defended the ad, repeating Trump’s claims that it had nothing to do with sexual abuse.

“We ran an ad about lying. Amy Acton is lying,” Ramaswamy told NBC News on Friday. “It had nothing to do with childhood abuse, which I will be the No. 1 governor to prosecute when I am the governor of this state because it is wrong.”

entries.title: Trump: Inquiry Into Top Advisers Is Dead After Presidential Library Donation
entries.summary: The president had publicly rebuked Chris LaCivita and James Blair over their work for a pro-Russian nationalist government in Bosnia-Herzegovina.
entries.content:
President Donald Trump said Friday that he is no longer looking into the outside consulting work conducted by a pair of his top political advisers after they donated to his presidential library.

Following reports of Chris LaCivita and James Blair’s consulting work for a pro-Russian nationalist government in Bosnia-Herzegovina, Trump vowed to investigate their work for foreign entities — going so far as to suggest that he might “terminate them” if any conflicts of interest were discovered.

But that was apparently settled shortly after the pair donated their full consulting fee from Republika Srpska, one of the two governing entities of Bosnia-Herzegovina, to Trump’s future presidential library. It’s unclear how much the donation was.

“They took the money and they gave it to essentially a charity,” Trump said. “I think it was a very nice thing to do.”

The donation was first reported Thursday evening by the New York Post.

LaCivita and Blair’s side hustle first garnered headlines after The New York Times reported that the two had traveled to Republika Srpska to advise its government on voting-related issues ahead of the country’s election earlier this month.

LaCivita co-led Trump’s 2024 presidential campaign and Blair served as a deputy chief of staff at the White House until his departure in May.

Republika Srpska is an autonomous entity that makes up half of Bosnia and Herzegovina, with a political leadership that includes pro-Russian Serb nationalists that have aligned themselves with Russian President Vladimir Putin. Its leaders have also spent heavily in recent years trying to court Trump and his supporters.

Trump rebuked both LaCivita and Blair publicly after learning about their foreign consulting work, writing on Truth Social: “If there’s a conflict, I will terminate them, immediately!”

Compounding matters, White House chief of staff Susie Wiles and her daughter, Katie Wiles, also met with senior figures of the region’s leadership in recent weeks.

CBS News reported that Katie Wiles traveled to Republika Srpska. A verified photo shows her holding a rifle next to the region’s interior minister, Željko Budimir.

A White House official told CBS News that “Susie does not discuss work matters with her daughters.”
entries.author: Michelle Del Rey

entries.title: White House: The First Lady Brokered a Temporary Ceasefire for a Besieged Ukrainian City
entries.summary: The agreement covers Oleshky, a small city occupied by Russia that the Vatican flagged last week as facing a humanitarian crisis.
entries.content:
The White House said Friday that first lady Melania Trump secured a ceasefire between Russia and Ukraine in a small front-line southern city.

Both countries agreed to temporarily halt military action beginning Oct. 29 to allow humanitarian aid into Oleshky, across the Dnipro River from Ukrainian-controlled Kherson, and to prepare a civilian evacuation through a designated safe passageway. The announcement does not say when the ceasefire ends.

The White House said the first lady and an unnamed representative worked directly with Russian and Ukrainian leadership to set the terms, acting in what it called her “formal role as Exclusive Intermediary.”

“It was abundantly clear that without my intervention, the possibility to bring humanitarian aid into the city and to evacuate the elderly would be impossible,” she said in the statement.

Residents who wish to leave “will receive coordinated support and transportation to their preferred destination,” she said. And “some will want to go to Russia, and some to Ukraine.”

Marc Beckman, who serves as a senior adviser to Melania Trump, said Friday in an interview with Newsmax that the agreement the first lady negotiated is the “first step towards everlasting peace between these two nations.”

Ostap Yarysh of Razom for Ukraine, a U.S.-based advocacy group, welcomed the announcement, saying humanitarian groups had sought an evacuation route for months as civilians endured severe shortages of food, water, electricity and medical care.

But he cautioned that Russia could use these sorts of token gestures, such as prisoner releases, to generate positive headlines, goodwill and the perception that it is engaging in the peace process.

“They basically take people hostage, and they release them and say, ‘Oh look, we engage in diplomacy,’” Yarysh said.

The White House statement notes the first lady secured an unnamed "impartial American media organization" to document Russian and Ukrainian teams on the ground. That outlet appears to be Newsmax, as an anchor on the conservative network claimed Friday morning that it was "the only network there" with cameras.

Bruno Cardoso Reis, a nonresident senior fellow in the Center on the United States and Europe at the Brookings Institution, said the arrangement is concerning. A media organization “lacks the expertise, experience and global legitimacy for this kind of job,” he said.

Oversight work typically is handled by trained observers stationed on both sides, he said, backed by intelligence capability, so that compliance can be verified and violations attributed. That is something the Red Cross and United Nations have long done.

Asked at a press gaggle Friday whether the first lady would be part of any future trilateral peace talks, President Donald Trump said no, “but it’s not the worst idea I’ve ever heard.”

“What she wants to do is save children, and that's her focus,” Trump said. “And both sides are cooperating with her.”

It was a sentiment echoed by at least one Trump administration official.

"Clearly the men weren't getting anywhere,” the official told The Washington Sun.

Pope Leo XIV requested a humanitarian ceasefire in the city from Russian President Vladimir Putin on Oct. 16, according to a Holy See statement. He called for a halt to allow food and medical assistance to reach Oleshky and for “the voluntary and safe evacuation of the civilian population.”

Putin told the pope he supported the Vatican initiative to help civilians in Oleshky and was ready to cooperate, Reuters reported last week.

The White House announcement did not say who will monitor compliance, nor does it detail how voluntary evacuations will be verified.

Cardoso Reis said Oleshky had become “a growing global embarrassment” that Putin could no longer ignore, and that he chose a route that paid him the most: moving from the Vatican’s channel to signal closeness to Trump and hand the president “a political win.” Still, he said, the pope and European leaders will welcome anyone who can help get aid in.

Russia’s war in Ukraine has surged back into the spotlight in recent weeks. Trump waived sanctions on Russia last week, telling reporters he was “in the midst of negotiating a deal” with Putin. The waiver was needed for a deal Trump had already struck for Russia to supply hundreds of thousands of tons of diesel in the coming months to tamp down the surging prices of the oil that powers much of the American economy.

He’s been pressed repeatedly this week on whether waiving sanctions to secure the release of detained American Stephen Hubbard amounted to a concession to Moscow.

He has also suggested Ukrainian President Volodymyr Zelenskyy should be replaced at the negotiating table.

“I think it’s time for somebody else to negotiate on behalf of Ukraine,” Trump told reporters Monday.Zelenskyy said Friday that restrictions affecting critical U.S. military support remained unresolved, even as the White House celebrated the diplomatic breakthrough over Oleshky.

Speaking to an audience at the Hudson Institute, Zelenskyy said Starlink and Starshield satellite services remained slowed, and shipments of air defense interceptors were still blocked.

The Office of the First Lady, the White House, the State Department and the Holy See Press Office did not respond to requests for comment.

Yarysh also credited the first lady with establishing a humanitarian channel through her efforts to reunite Ukrainian children with their families, calling the Oleshky agreement a potentially positive development. Her work, he said, has resulted in more than two dozen children returning to their families.

“Of course, we’ll have to see whether Russia adheres to that [agreement] and complies with everything,” he said.

entries.title: Feds Stop Evidence Sharing in Good and Pretti Killings: Minnesota Officials
entries.summary: The state is still seeking the cell phones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.
entries.content:
By Hannah Schoenbaum

The federal government has stopped sharing evidence with Minnesota authorities who are investigating the killings of Renee Good and Alex Pretti by federal officers, state officials said in recent court filings.

Minnesota officials sued President Donald Trump's administration in March for access to materials they said they needed to independently investigate the shootings during Trump’s immigration crackdown in Minneapolis earlier this year. The Trump administration has suggested that state prosecutors don’t have jurisdiction to investigate federal officers, while Minnesota officials have said they don’t trust the federal government to investigate itself.

The state is still seeking the cell phones of the officers involved in both shootings and recordings of key interviews.

State prosecutors announced in July that the federal government had begun turning over evidence in the cases, including police body camera video and hard drives containing statements. Hennepin County Attorney Mary Moriarty said at the time that the state expected to receive “all the evidence.”

But Minnesota investigators said in October court filings that the transfer of evidence stopped soon after the July announcement. Moriarty said the U.S. Attorney’s Office for Minnesota told her on Sept. 10 that evidence sharing would be on pause indefinitely “in light of challenges with D.C.," according to the documents.

State prosecutors have again asked a judge to order federal agencies to hand over the evidence, arguing they "have identified no legal authority or rational basis justifying their obstruction of state criminal investigations."

In a reply filed Tuesday, attorneys for the Justice Department argued it's within their discretion to decline to share information with state authorities. They cited the department's rules for responding to record requests, known as the Touhy regulations, which apply only when formal legal proceedings are underway. The attorneys said there was no active court case when Minnesota made its requests.

Drew Evans, superintendent of the Minnesota Bureau of Criminal Apprehension, said in a legal declaration that federal authorities still have Good’s clothing, the cell phone of the officer who killed her and interview recordings that state authorities have never been able to view.

An Immigration and Customs Enforcement officer fatally shot Good, a 37-year-old mother of three, while she was leaving a Minneapolis protest on Jan. 7. Bystander video shows Good in the driver’s seat of an SUV, repeatedly honking the horn, when masked immigration officers order her to step out of the vehicle. She starts to pull forward, and an officer standing in front of the car fires at her windshield. The officer, now standing about an arm’s length from the open window on the driver's side, fires twice more, according to an analysis of the videos by The Associated Press and others.

Federal officials at the time said the officer acted in self-defense.

Good's death and that of Pretti, a 37-year-old intensive care nurse who was killed weeks later by a federal officer in Minneapolis, ignited nationwide protests against the Republican president's immigration enforcement efforts.

No criminal charges have been filed in connection with the fatal shootings.

Evans said the federal government also has not shared a recorded statement from an officer who shot Pretti, the firearms used by the officers, their phones, projectiles and casings, and a gun taken from Pretti before he was shot.

entries.title: Susan Collins Says She Convinced the Trump Administration to Lift Some Tariffs on Canada
entries.summary: The development comes as polling continues to find the Maine senator in a close race with her Democratic opponent, Troy Jackson.
entries.content:
Sen. Susan Collins, who is currently locked in a tight race for reelection, said on Friday that she had convinced White House officials to exempt certain Canadian agricultural products from President Donald Trump’s tariffs.

The Republican senator has been vocal about how the U.S.’s trade war with Canada could affect residents of Maine and other states that border the country’s northern neighbor. The reductions come just over a week before Election Day, when Collins and other battleground Senate candidates will face tight reelection races — and as voters’ concerns about high prices reach a fever pitch.

Collins listed a number of items that would soon be exempted from Trump’s 50% tariffs, including certain paper and plastic packaging, refrigeration and freezing equipment, agricultural cleaning products, labeling and wrapping machinery and seaweed and algae products, among other agricultural supplies.

Maine’s blueberry, potato and apple growers rely on harvesting boxes from Canada that help bring produce to market, Collins’ office said in a news release.

The situation became urgent after an American supplier of cardboard totes recently discontinued production, forcing producers to turn to Canada, the senator wrote.

“These producers are a vital part of our state’s economy and support our rural and coastal communities,” Collins said.

She added that a tariff on Canadian seaweed has already put dozens of Maine jobs at risk.

Collins previously secured tariff exemptions for pulp, road salt, cement and American seafood.

In September, Canada imposed retaliatory tariffs of 15%, 25%, and 50% on steel, dairy, appliances, agricultural equipment, pulp and paper and electronics, according to the Canadian government’s website, after Trump announced in July that he’d be imposing a 50% tariff on select Canadian goods.

The U.S. tariffs went into effect in August.

The Canadian tariffs are the largest the Trump administration has placed on any country since the Supreme Court limited Trump’s tariff authority in February.

In a phone call with reporters, a senior administration official said, “These tariffs are in response to discriminatory mistreatment by Canada against U.S. products.”

The official specifically cited Canada’s decision to limit the sale of American liquor in Canadian government-owned liquor stores and to put quotas on American vehicles and dairy products.

Section 338 of the Tariff Act of 1930 allows the president to impose tariffs on countries that discriminate against U.S. commerce, they continued.

“These are defensive measures by the United States taken to remedy discriminatory actions by Canada, as the president has made very clear,” the official said. “Both in his campaign and during his administration for the past year and a half, the United States has taken action to protect its national security and to rebalance trade.”

entries.title: Two Ex-FBI Agents Are Arrested as the Hunter Biden Laptop Scandal Returns
entries.summary: Republicans have long alleged that the pair lied to Congress ahead of the 2020 election.
entries.content:
The Hunter Biden laptop saga is back with a vengeance, with the Justice Department on Friday criminally charging two former high-ranking FBI agents with lying to Congress — settling a long-running score for Republicans who felt the pair had impeded their attempt to make the scandal a decisive issue in the 2020 election.

Jeanine Pirro, the U.S. attorney for the District of Columbia, announced that both former bureau officials surrendered Friday after arrest warrants were issued in a legal complaint filed Tuesday. The investigation was led out of the FBI’s Kansas field office.

The former agents ran the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force, which was created in 2017 under then-Director Christopher Wray in the aftermath of Russia’s attempts to influence the 2016 election by maligning Democratic presidential candidate Hillary Clinton. It was disbanded weeks after President Donald Trump returned to the White House last year, as part of his transformation of the FBI.

Nikki Floris, 46, was the task force’s assistant director, and Bradley Benavides, 56, was its section chief. After their tenure on that team, both were pulled into House Judiciary Committee Chair Jim Jordan’s yearslong crusade to probe the business activities of President Joe Biden’s son.

The inquiry dates back to an incident in which Hunter Biden left his laptop at a Wilmington, Delaware, computer repair shop in 2019, only to have it turned over to MAGA stalwart Rudy Giuliani. The former New York City mayor handed it to the FBI, and the saga eventually blew up into a scandal following a New York Post story in the closing weeks of the 2020 presidential election alleging improper political influence tied to Hunter Biden’s business interests in Ukraine.

Floris and Benavides “knew about and were actively involved in the FBI’s investigations of Hunter Biden” but repeatedly feigned ignorance when answering the Judiciary Committee’s questions during two interviews in 2023, according to a 27-page affidavit written by FBI Special Agent Byron Militello, a longtime investigator at the bureau in the Midwest.

The affidavit alleges that Floris was directly involved with the way the bureau fielded press inquiries following the Post’s story on Oct. 14, 2020, and even approved additions to

Wray’s talking points about the matter for a call with Sen. Mark Warner (D-Virginia). And it points to her conflicting answer in 2023 when the House Judiciary Committee asked how long the FBI had the laptop.

“I don’t know what laptop the article was referring to,” it quotes her as saying.

The affidavit also cites messages between Benavides and a person who appears to have been the assistant special agent in charge of the Baltimore field office, in which they discuss when exactly the laptop was seized and whether emails on it were shared with agents in New York. However, the affidavit says, Benavides told Jordan’s committee otherwise.

“I was made aware per the Wikipedia article that the FBI had taken possession of a

laptop circa December of 2019,” it quotes him saying in a transcript.

“Okay. You didn’t have that knowledge from your role in the FBI?” he was asked.

“Absolutely not,” he responded, according to the transcript.

Court records show that Floris is being represented by several lawyers including Margaret Donovan, a Connecticut attorney who is representing several FBI agents being targeted by the Trump administration. Benavides’ lawyer is Kimberly Paschall, who until last year was a senior attorney in the same D.C. office now prosecuting her client and has publicly signed on to a letter protesting what it calls the weaponization of the DOJ. Paschall did not respond to a request for comment.

Donovan and Washington Litigation Group lawyers Mary Dohrmann and Kyle Freeny put out a statement calling Floris “a patriot.”

“She served our nation as a dedicated FBI intelligence officer for nearly 20 years. Yet today, the DOJ has accused her falsely of a crime on the say-so of politicians, not on the facts. It’s no coincidence the government is filing these nonsense charges now, years later, on the eve of an election,” they wrote. “The government’s reasons for charging Nikki are as transparent as they are unjust: to push a false narrative for a shot at political points. It’s another sad day for the DOJ, but we look forward to Nikki’s day in court.”

The current case stems from the Republican Party’s unfinished business with Hunter Biden, who faced decades in prison after being convicted of an illegal gun purchase and tax dodging — until he was pardoned by his father, the president. For years, Senate Judiciary Committee Chair Chuck Grassley has publicly complained that Floris and Benavides had become a speedbump in his attempt to draw attention to the Biden scandal during the closing months of the 2020 presidential election, which Trump ultimately lost.

At a time when Republicans were trying to pin then-candidate Joe Biden as a former vice president whose influence helped his son benefit from corrupt business dealings in Ukraine, Democrats were trying to cast the entire affair as a mere Russian foreign influence operation.

In the midst of that scramble, according to Republicans, Democratic Sens. Gary Peters of Michigan and Ron Wyden of Oregon requested that the FBI’s Foreign Influence Task Force brief the Judiciary and Homeland Security committees about what they claimed was Russia’s attempt to sway the presidential election.

That briefing, which is mentioned in a GOP report, eventually came on Aug. 6, 2020. As Republicans tell it, that hearing derailed their congressional investigation into Hunter Biden by marring it as the spoils of a Russian disinformation campaign.

“That FBI task force was involved in unnecessarily briefing us two senators,” Grassley said last year, referring to himself and Sen. Ron Johnson (R-Wisconsin. “But that only happened after pressure from our Democratic colleagues. So, pure and simple, this was a setup,”

“The contents of that briefing were later leaked to the media, even though the FBI promised us confidentiality,” he continued. “Those leaks were used to falsely link our Biden family investigation to somehow advancing Russian disinformation. The FBI’s conduct undermined and frustrated our congressional investigation.”

Grassley released a statement Friday that called Floris and Benavides “two unelected bureaucrats” who “used the power of government to smear my and Senator Johnson’s constitutional oversight and distract from inconvenient truths that weaponized bureaucrats and the Biden administration didn’t want you to know.”

The FBI affidavit unsealed Friday references that interaction and the way it later led to a House Judiciary probe under Jordan, whose committee interviewed Floris on July 19, 2023, and Benavides on Sept. 28, 2023. According to the affidavit, Floris described herself during that testimony as the FBI’s election security lead during the 2020 presidential election.

The affidavit quotes the House Judiciary Committee asking her, “Was there ever a discussion at the [Foreign Influence Task Force] about Hunter Biden?” To which she responded: “No. At least not with me. And again, there’s a whole team below me, so whether or not conversations happened, I don’t know, but I personally did not have any conversations.”

However, the affidavit alleges that Floris and Benavides oversaw how the task force “informally formed a group of analysts to work on a project later known as ‘Round River,’” which is described as a group that was “scrutinizing informant intelligence relating to the Hunter Biden investigations as potential disinformation.”

Wyden’s office shot back on Friday afternoon.

“The idea that the Russian disinformation narrative was fabricated by the Foreign Influence Task Force is a conspiracy theory. As the Wyden-Peters report lays out, the overwhelming evidence shows that the Grassley Johnson investigation advanced a Russian disinformation campaign in an effort to affect the outcome of the 2020 presidential election,” senior Wyden aide Keith Chu told The Washington Sun.



The first Trump administration’s own Treasury Department sanctioned Ukrainian politician Andrii Derkach and others for their role in the Hunter Biden affair and attempt to influence the U.S. presidential election, noting that Derkach had “been an active Russian agent for over a decade, maintaining close connections with the Russian Intelligence Services.”

entries.title: Researchers Call Out the Irony in Melania Trump’s Women’s Health Push
entries.summary: The call for investment in women’s health research contradicts staffing and budget cuts at the nation’s health and research agencies, researchers say.
entries.content:
First lady Melania Trump’s new initiative to advance research in women’s health has some women’s health researchers scratching their heads.

The Trump administration’s approach to federal grant funding and demographic-specific research — including freezing billions in health research funds and banning diversity, equity and inclusion programs — has taken a toll on those doing the very work the Trump administration now says it wants to prioritize, these researchers said.

“I have a whole lab of junior investigators and early-career investigators that I mentor, and some of them left academia feeling very discouraged that their research would not get funded or that they could not have a career in this area,” said Dr. Crystal Schiller, who leads a lab at the University of North Carolina studying women’s neuroscience. “And that was very disheartening.”

Schiller said she’s still “very happy” to see the administration identify women’s health research as a priority.

Melania Trump’s new initiative and President Donald Trump’s coinciding executive order establishing a White House women’s health task force and a women’s health division at the National Institutes of Health, expressed a “commitment to advancing women’s health and ensuring that medical research, diagnosis, prevention, and treatment reflect the highest quality of scientific evidence.”

The administration’s slash-and-burn approach to federal funding, however, is still fresh on many researchers’ minds. Research around women’s health was particularly hard hit, according to Dr. Jane Salmon, a rheumatologist and professor of medicine at Weill Cornell Medicine.

“We lost people to industry. We admitted fewer students because of lab resource losses and insecurity about supporting [students],” Salmon said. “There was an environment of no security. It created a culture of anxiety and a low threshold for departures.”

The Trump administration has laid off thousands of federal public health workers and proposed cutting NIH’s budget by 12%. An analysis by the liberal think tank Center for American Program found the administration had eliminated at least $3 billion in women’s health research grants.

In March of 2025, NIH began canceling grants for research projects related to diversity, equity and inclusion. In the year that followed, the NIH saw a 31% decline in projects that included the word “women,” according to reporting from The Washington Post.

In a statement to The Sun, White House spokeswoman Allison Schuster said that improving health for Americans was a “top priority for President Trump and the First Lady” and that the new task force “will work to close critical research gaps and strengthen care for women across all stages of life.”

Researchers told The Washington Sun that women’s health has historically been underfunded and understudied, from a lack of inclusion in clinical trials to studying treatments for conditions that disproportionately or more severely affect women. In 2025, a consensus study report published by the National Academies of Sciences, Engineering, and Medicine recommended that Congress invest $11.4 billion into women’s health research over five years. The executive order from the Trump administration does not say how it will fund the investment it calls for.

“Any effort to increase attention to funding for those things is a good thing,” said Sheila Burke, a health care policy adviser and co-chair of the NASEM committee that authored the report. “The concern I had was there was no mention of money.”

The NIH already has an Office of Research on Women’s Health, but the office does not have its own research budget and must coordinate across all 27 of the agency’s institutes.

Former first lady Jill Biden also formed a White House Initiative on Women’s Health Research during her tenure. The initiative was followed by an executive order from President Joe Biden saying “we know far too little about women’s health across women’s lifespans.”

Unlike the Trump administration’s task force, the Biden administration’s order directed the head of the Office of Management and Budget to participate in its task force, implying that the initiative would be considered in budget talks. The Trump-defined task force does not include the head of OMB.

The Biden administration did not secure a congressional budget for women’s health research at the NIH. Katie Keith, former deputy director of the White House Gender Policy Council who oversaw Jill Biden’s initiative, said that the Biden Women’s Health Initiative pooled resources across government agencies and was “able to galvanize almost a billion dollars ourselves.”

Keith said that the Biden initiative worked with the National Science Foundation, the Agency for Healthcare Research and Quality, the Substance Abuse and Mental Health Services Administration, and several other agencies not named in the Trump executive order. These agencies experienced significant staffing and funding losses in DOGE cuts.

“Watching all those cuts and having entire divisions that worked on women’s health-related issues, in some instances, be gutted I think was a huge setback to this effort that they say they now want to prioritize,” Keith said.

The Biden initiative was led by Dr. Carolyn Mazure, a professor of psychiatry and founding director of the Women’s Health Research group at Yale School of Medicine.

Trump’s task force will be co-chaired by Health and Human Services Secretary Robert F. Kennedy Jr. and White House chief of staff Susie Wiles.

Trump said that his motivation for announcing an investment in women’s health was inspired by Melania Trump. In the White House Rose Garden, Trump said, “When I heard about it, I said, ‘Are you sure they don’t have that?’ Who the hell wouldn’t have a women’s health division?”

The NIH’s Office of Research on Women’s Health was established in 1993 and makes up less than half a percent of the agency’s budget.

entries.title: The Pentagon Says It’s Letting Wind Projects Continue. Wind Companies Say Otherwise.
entries.summary: The future of these projects could impact Congress’ permitting reform negotiations.
entries.content:
The Trump administration said this week that it will move forward on two onshore wind projects and begin working on other projects waiting for approvals, after long delays by the Defense Department. In court filings, wind companies say the agency has perpetuated delays instead of restarting a review process they were ordered to resume.

On Thursday, the White House said it would unblock two onshore wind projects in Maine and South Dakota in an attempt to pave the way for a permitting reform bill’s passage, Punchbowl reported.

The Defense Department was ordered in August to move projects awaiting approvals forward as part of a lawsuit brought by trade associations, wind energy companies and environmental organizations. In court filings from earlier this week, those groups said the agency is “maintaining its review freeze through new mechanisms” and asked a judge to enforce that order.

The future of these wind projects weigh heavily on ongoing negotiations around the future of American energy infrastructure. A bipartisan group of senators is trying to wrangle votes for a permitting reform bill that could expedite wind-energy development across the country. But the Trump administration’s attempts to block clean energy infrastructure have presented a challenge for some Democrats.

Earlier this week, the Trump administration’s efforts to reconsider a federal permit granted to an offshore wind farm — the fourth such effort in recent months — renewed those concerns. Sen. Sheldon Whitehouse (D-Rhode Island), one of the lead negotiators of the permitting bill, said the White House’s moves could derail permitting reform talks.

Whitehouse called the two onshore projects advancing a “start.”

More than 300 wind projects are under review by the Defense Department, a process meant to assess whether energy infrastructure will have an impact on military operations and identify ways to mitigate those impacts. The agency gradually stopped doing those reviews in August 2025.

Lawyers for the Pentagon have asked for the onshore wind case to be dismissed, arguing concerns about national security should take precedence over energy developers’ interests.

Citing drone warfare in Iran and Ukraine, defense officials said a freeze was necessary because of advancing “adversarial capabilities” and global threats. The agency has said it needs to reassess the review process for projects that could cause “impactful Doppler interference,” a category that only applies to wind turbines.

At a hearing in late September, a government lawyer told the judge that reviews for wind projects have resumed but was not able to provide specific examples of projects moving forward. More recently, federal lawyers said the Pentagon has resumed “processing” wind energy applications and began applying a new methodology to “capture emergent threats.”

The groups suing the Defense Department said in court filings on Tuesday that none of the agreements previously negotiated with wind projects have been signed. Instead of signing them, the Pentagon has created a new 119-page mitigation agreement that includes new requirements including vetting personnel and supply chains — an expansion from the roughly 20-page agreement previously used.

The Defense Department did not respond to The Washington Sun’s questions about whether the two wind projects have official, signed agreements that would allow them to move forward.

The new requirements aren’t related to the radar and drone concerns the agency has voiced, the groups argued in their filing.

“DoD is proposing to impose these new requirements across all wind projects, without either identifying which (if any) particular adverse impacts to military operations or readiness warrant their application to individual projects or explaining why the mitigation measures already agreed upon for these projects are inadequate,” the filing says.

The groups asked a judge to force the Pentagon to either sign agreements that had already been negotiated, or provide detailed reasons for not addressing potential adverse impacts on military operations.

For projects in the earlier stages of review, the Defense Department has invited some project developers to negotiate, but wind companies say they have mostly received requests for time extensions.

The review delays have caused some wind developers to abandon or shift their projects, the groups suing the Pentagon say.

entries.title: Buttigieg Endorses a Montana Independent Over His Democratic Opponent
entries.summary: Many Democrats in the state believe Seth Bodnar will have a better chance of victory in Montana — historically a GOP stronghold.
entries.content:
Pete Buttigieg, the former transportation secretary and Democratic 2028 presidential hopeful, endorsed an independent candidate for U.S. Senate in Montana over their Democratic opponent, joining other members of the party who have backed independents in races across the country.

In a video announcement posted on X Friday, Buttigieg highlighted Seth Bodnar’s military service — the 47-year-old was an Army Green Beret who served in Iraq as a patrol leader in 2008. His history of military service is one he shares with Buttigieg, who served as Navy Reserve intelligence officer in Afghanistan.

“Seth and I don't agree on everything,” Buttigieg said in the video. “ But at a time when Washington is more broken than ever, we need people like Seth who do the right thing and have the courage to work with anyone.”

“Thats what service teaches you,” Buttigieg continued. “Mission first, take care of others, and never forget who you work for. Seth knows who he works for.”

Bodnar enthusiastically accepted Buttigieg’s backing in his own statement, writing that he was “proud that people across the political spectrum are joining this campaign.”

“We agree that Washington, D.C. is broken,” Bodnar wrote on X. “And it’s time we take our country back from politicians and party bosses who enable the corruption driving up costs for all of us.”

Bodnar is running against Republican candidate Kurt Alme and Democratic candidate Alani Bankhead. Many Democrats in the state believe Bodnar will have a better chance of victory in Montana — historically a GOP stronghold.

Earlier this week Bankhead told PBS that the DNC offered her a job at the committee if she dropped out of the race. The DNC has since denied those claims.

Buttigieg, who plans to campaign in seven states ahead of the midterm elections, is a major Democratic figure and one of the favorites to run for the presidency in 2028. With his endorsement of Bodnar, he joins other Democrats who have backed independents in races nationwide.

entries.title: State Department Press Adviser Resigns After Altercation at Washington Wizards Game
entries.summary: Britt McHenry was reportedly promoted and fired within 24 hours.
entries.content:
A State Department press adviser was forced to resign after she was captured on video chucking a drink at a fan at a Washington Wizards game this week.

Britt McHenry, 40, began working at the department in September. She had previously written for The Spectator and worked as a news anchor at Fox News and ESPN, according to her LinkedIn page.

Page Six was first to report McHenry’s resignation. She confirmed to Front Office Sports that she had signed a resignation letter.

“She was forced to resign [over the incident],” an unnamed source told Page Six. “She was promoted and fired within 24 hours.”

The Washington Sun has contacted McHenry for comment.

The State Department told The Sun it does not “comment on internal personnel matters.”

The saga began at Capital One Arena during the Wizards’ season opener against the Milwaukee Bucks on Wednesday.

Page Six reported that a fan began “heckling” former Wizards player Kyle Kuzma, who now plays for the Bucks and is engaged to supermodel Winnie Harlow. Harlow has vitiligo, a chronic autoimmune condition that causes the varied loss of skin pigmentation throughout the body.

“They were saying he plays terribly because his girlfriend’s ugly,” a source told Page Six.

McHenry told the fan to “ease up,” prompting attendees to turn their attention to her.

Footage obtained by TMZ shows McHenry chucking a drink into a man’s face as fans chanted, “Get her out!” She exited the stadium blowing kisses and waving at attendees. Fans threw items at McHenry as she left her seat.

The State Department hired McHenry to be a press adviser covering Europe and Africa, Page Six reported. On the day of the incident, she’d been promoted to a new position.

She previously handled media relations over a scandal involving Kimberly Guilfoyle, in which she alledgely asked a Trump donor to cover $100,000 in credit card expenses before she was confirmed as U.S. ambassador to Greece, the outlet reported. Guilfoyle resigned Oct. 13.

According to the outlet, ESPN suspended McHenry in 2015 after footage of her lashing out at a towing company employee went viral.

“Do you feel good about your job? So I could be a college dropout and do the same thing? Why, ’cause I have a brain, and you don’t?” she said in the video as her car was being towed. “Maybe if I was missing some teeth, they would hire me, huh? … ‘Cause I’m on television, and you’re in a fucking trailer, honey.”

entries.title: New Kimberly Guilfoyle Financial Report Illuminates Debts
entries.summary: The former U.S. ambassador reported mortgage and boat liabilities — but no credit card debt — amid allegations of financial misconduct she denies.
entries.content:
Recently resigned U.S. Ambassador to Greece Kimberly Guilfoyle disclosed sizable mortgage and boat loans among her personal liabilities, but no credit card debt entering 2026, according to an unpublished federal ethics document obtained by The Washington Sun from the State Department.

Guilfoyle resigned her ambassadorship on Oct. 13 amid accusations of financial misconduct, which she denies, and pressure from President Donald Trump and the White House.

The Wall Street Journal reported Guilfoyle asked Republican donor Eric Deters to spot her $100,000 to cover an American Express credit card bill before her Senate confirmation in September 2025. In exchange for the money, Guilfoyle promised access to senior officials in the administration, the Journal reported. She is also accused of improperly accepting gifts.

Guilfoyle denied taking part in a “pay-to-play” scheme, writing on X: “These allegations are false, and I intend to vigorously defend my name, my reputation, and my integrity.”

The ethics document indicates Guilfoyle has a boat loan from 2024 valued at between $100,001 and $250,000 and a 5-year-old mortgage valued at between $1 million and $5 million.

Guilfoyle did not list credit card debt on either her new financial disclosure, which she originally filed in May and remains under review at the State Department, or a financial disclosure she submitted last year prior to her confirmation.

Guilfoyle did list an “exercised line of credit” worth between $250,001 and $500,000 from RBC Wealth Management on her older financial disclosure that did not appear on the new disclosure.

Guilfoyle could not be reached for comment Friday. The U.S. Embassy in Greece referred questions to the State Department, which along with the Office of Government Ethics did not respond to The Sun’s request for comment.

Guilfoyle’s latest financial disclosure lists significant personal assets, including a podcast company and consulting businesses.

Her podcast company reportedly earned $1.5 million during 2025, while a consulting business generated about $250,000.

She valued ownership stakes in two other companies — Polished Rice Inc. and Metropolitan Medspa LLC — at between $1 million and $5 million each, although she reported no income from them last year.

Government officials are only required to disclose assets and debts in broad ranges, making it difficult to determine Guilfoyle’s exact personal net worth.

In compliance with the ethics agreement she signed in May 2025, before her confirmation, Guilfoyle sold dozens of individual stock holdings and appeared to reinvest the money into exchange-traded, mutual and index funds. She also reported that during her ambassadorial service, most of her businesses would be inactive or involve her only as a passive owner.

In December 2024, Trump indicated he would nominate Guilfoyle — his son Donald Trump Jr.’s former fiancée — for an ambassadorship, and he officially nominated her in early 2025.

But following her confirmation, her tenure lasted little more than a year.

“We’re not happy,” CNN reported Trump telling reporters the day before Guilfoyle's departure.

Deters filed a defamation lawsuit against Guilfoyle last week. In a statement to CNN, Guilfoyle’s lawyers said Deters owed Guilfoyle money for speeches and consulting work.

entries.title: Work Trucks at East Potomac Park Are Seen With Covered Logos and License Plates
entries.summary: The video taken Thursday morning follows Trump administration claims that tree removals at the park aren't linked to the president's golf course plans.

Trucks seen at East Potomac Park on Thursday had their license plates and the name of their business covered, in apparent violation of local and federal transportation law.

Photos and videos posted on social media by D.C. photographer Andrew Leyden showed the trucks being used to haul away debris, he said in the posts.

Under D.C. law, covering license plates is illegal. The U.S. Department of Transportation requires commercial vehicles to display the operator’s name and Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration identification number on both sides.

The photos and videos of the trucks come after tumultuous exchanges this week between the Trump administration’s lawyers and a federal judge over the president’s efforts to redevelop the public golf course into a “world class championship” facility.
Truck (4096x2304, AR: 1.78)On Monday, U.S. District Judge Ana Reyes questioned the administration’s claim that removing hundreds of trees from East Potomac Golf Links was unrelated to President Donald Trump’s project.

The week before, Reyes ordered the redevelopment to halt until at least Oct. 26 after the government carried out a massive tree-cutting at the golf course with little notice to the court or plaintiffs.

Trump announced on social media Sunday that the golf course would close for 15 months for the project, starting Nov. 15. Hours later, the administration argued in a court filing that no plans for the construction project are final and they should not be subject to judicial review.

“There is no universe in which all of this coincidentally happened all at the same time,” Reyes said Monday.

Trump has bashed the current state of the golf course and the surrounding park areas, calling it “Trash Island” and arguing that redevelopment would attract high-level professional golf tournaments and create jobs.

In a statement to The Washington Sun, Andy Ross, president of Ross Tree Expert Company, which has a current contract for work on the park, said “the vehicle pictured is not RTEC Treecare and has no affiliation” with the company. He said the company’s work at the park involved removal of specific hazardous and invasive trees and “did not include recent mass removals of trees.”

Another company with a contract for work on East Potomac Park, Vanasse Hangen Brustlin Inc., did not respond to a request for comment Friday evening.

The Interior Department, National Park Service, U.S. Department of Transportation and Federal Motor Carrier Safety Administration did not respond to requests for comment.

The D.C. Preservation League, which sued in February to stop the project, also did not respond to a request for comment.

This story has been updated to include a statement from Ross Tree Expert Company.
